#6368. Webb reveals the hidden activity inside a turbulent stellar nursery

Webb peers through thick cosmic dust in NGC 7129, revealing hidden young stars, protostars, glowing gas, and powerful outflows.

Today’s Image of the Day from the European Space Agency reveals a stellar nursery where young stars are changing the clouds that gave birth to them.

The James Webb Space Telescope captured NGC 7129, a star-forming region about 3,300 light-years from Earth.

Thick clouds of gas and dust obscure much of the activity at visible wavelengths.

Webb’s infrared vision can penetrate that material, bringing previously hidden stars and structures into view.

The result shows much more than a collection of newborn stars. NGC 7129 contains objects at several stages of early stellar development.

Some are still gathering material. Others have moved closer to the long, stable period of life that includes stars such as our Sun.

Stars do not all mature at the same rate. More massive stars generally form and evolve faster than smaller ones.

That difference allows astronomers to study several chapters of stellar development within the same region.

The brightest central star in this scene is LkH(alpha) 234. It has about five to eight times the mass of the Sun and produces the image’s most noticeable diffraction pattern.

It is a pre-main-sequence star, meaning it has largely finished collecting mass but has not yet begun the sustained hydrogen fusion that will define its main-sequence life.

At this stage, gravity continues to pull the star inward. As it contracts, its interior grows hotter.

Eventually, conditions in the core will become intense enough for hydrogen fusion to begin.

This transition matters because a young star does not develop quietly.

Even before reaching the main sequence, it can send powerful streams of material into the gas around it.

Those outflows can reshape a stellar nursery across surprisingly large distances.

The clearest evidence appears to the left of LkH(alpha) 234. A golden cavity stretches roughly 3.5 light-years across.

Outflows produced during an earlier stage of the star’s development carved into the surrounding molecular cloud, which consists largely of hydrogen.

Radiation and outflowing material from the star energize the gas and make it glow.

Some gas gets swept away, but the process does not simply shut down star formation.

Other material becomes compressed. Dense pockets can then provide the conditions needed for additional stars to develop.

Several young stars are visible inside the cavity. Some are also pre-main-sequence stars, and they produce stellar winds of their own.

As these winds push into surrounding gas, they create curved structures called bow shocks.

The stars also create a hot environment beside colder, denser molecular material. The boundary between these environments is known as a photodissociation region.

Energetic radiation breaks hydrogen molecules apart into individual atoms there.

The process changes the chemistry, heating and cooling of the cloud and helps determine how it evolves.

Molecular clouds are the raw material for star formation, but the stars born inside them gradually help destroy them.

Radiation, winds, and outflows can disperse gas or alter its chemistry.

Over millions of years, those effects can erode the cloud and change where new stars are able to form.

NGC 7129 gives astronomers a particularly useful view of that process because its stars have reached different developmental stages.

Their combined activity shows how star formation can both disrupt a cloud and compress parts of it into conditions favorable for further stellar growth.

The right side of Webb’s image tells an earlier part of the story.

Clumpy red material conceals protostars that are younger than the pre-main-sequence stars visible elsewhere in the region.

Protostars form after cold molecular gas and dust collapse and fragment into dense concentrations.

They continue gaining mass from surrounding material.

At the same time, they can eject narrow, extremely hot outflows that slam into the dense matter around them.

Those collisions produce shocks within the gray material surrounding the protostars.

They help create the textured appearance seen by Webb and contribute to the region’s red glow.

Several protostars are active at once, so their outflows overlap from Earth’s viewpoint. That makes this side of NGC 7129 look especially tangled.

Yet the apparent disorder contains valuable information about stars that would otherwise remain hidden behind dust.

Infrared observations give astronomers access to these deeply embedded objects before they emerge from their birth clouds.

In NGC 7129, Webb captures stars at different points along that path while also revealing how strongly they affect their surroundings.

The nursery will continue changing as its young stars mature.

Gas will disperse, dense pockets may collapse, and some newly formed stars will eventually settle into the hydrogen-fusing stage that powers the Sun today.

#6366. MIT researchers built a tiny new computer from squishy materials that works like a human brain

A soft film 2 nanometers thick lets a tiny device hold a memory for seconds and then fire like a neuron, all within one part.

Computers left moving parts behind a long time ago, trading gears and wheels for electrons flowing through chips that don’t change shape.

At a size far smaller than a single brain cell, a new device goes back to motion. Once squeezed, it takes a few seconds to recover its shape, so it can add up signals and fire, like an artificial neuron.

Because of that delay, one tiny part holds a short memory and acts on it. That job usually takes extra components such as capacitors.

Farnaz Niroui, an associate professor in MIT’s Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS) and a member of its Research Laboratory of Electronics (RLE), led the team that built it. Chemist Jeremiah Johnson of MIT’s Department of Chemistry joined them.

It’s a laboratory demonstration, and its biggest energy savings are a projection rather than a measurement.

Part of the inspiration came from animals that handle information where it arrives. For example, many of an octopus’s nerve cells are in its arms, which can sense and respond without waiting on the brain.

“You can think of an octopus as continuous computing matter, with computing, memory, sensing, and actuation distributed throughout its body,” Niroui said.

Mechanical computing goes back at least to the gears of the ancient Antikythera mechanism.

Modern mechanical computers have mostly stayed at the scale of millimeters. Shrinking them further runs into a basic problem. Surfaces brought within a few billionths of a meter of each other pull together and stick.

To get around it, the researchers laid a soft polymer film called PDMS, about 2 nanometers thick, between two gold electrodes.

Each device’s working area is a square 200 nanometers on a side, so more than 20 of them could fit across even a small neuron.

The top electrode is free to move. When the researchers applied a voltage, the two electrodes pulled toward each other and squeezed the film. More current crosses a thinner gap, so the current rose as the film thinned.

Niroui described the film as a “nano-spring” that keeps the metal surfaces from collapsing together for good. From the current, the team calculated that the gap shrank from about 2.3 nanometers to 1.6 nanometers.

They confirmed the squeeze with light. As the voltage rose, light scattered off a device shifted toward red, while a copy built with a stiff ceramic layer instead of PDMS showed no shift.

Peter Satterthwaite, a graduate student who co-led the work with fellow graduate student Sarah Spector, explained why that matters.

“PDMS is viscoelastic, which means that after being compressed, it takes time to return to its original state,” Satterthwaite said.

“This allows the devices to dynamically remember the history of forces and voltages applied to them, and convert that history into an electrical response.”

A pulse lasting 50 milliseconds squeezed the film by about 8 percent, and the current recovered as soon as the voltage stopped. A pulse 10 times longer squeezed it by about 30 percent, and the current returned gradually over several seconds.

So what the device does now depends on what happened to it a few seconds ago. When the team waited only half a second between tests instead of 40 seconds, the film hadn’t fully recovered, and the tests started from a narrower gap.

A neuron in the brain collects incoming signals a little at a time. If they arrive slowly, the charge drains away. If they arrive close together, the charge builds past a threshold, and the neuron fires a signal to its neighbors before resetting.

The neuron device did the same thing. The team sent it a string of 2.5-volt pulses, each too weak to trigger it alone, spaced closer together than the film could recover. After 16 pulses, the current jumped, and the device then relaxed back to where it started.

“We have this complex functionality, which is the basis of biological computing, all contained in one nanoscale device,” he said.

Its memory lasts seconds, while most other artificial neurons hold theirs for millionths or thousandths of a second. The team wrote that this suits tasks that need context over a few seconds.

The researchers also wired two devices to one shared resistor. Once the first device fired, the second couldn’t fire until the first had relaxed, the way one active neuron in a brain can hold back its neighbor.

As built, the device used 54 nanojoules of energy in tests. By the team’s calculation, it only needs to store about 2 femtojoules of electrical energy each time it fires, and a femtojoule is a millionth of a nanojoule.

At 200 nanometers across, the device is more than 100 times smaller than a typical neuron. Cut the current that leaks through it and shrink it further, the team wrote, and it could beat a real neuron on energy efficiency.

The team presented that kind of efficiency as a way to meet the growing demands of artificial intelligence.

“The performance highly relies on the memory introduced using the soft polymer,” Spector said. “We can intentionally engineer this over a large design space to meet the requirements of the desired applications.”

Every measurement was made in a lab, on devices kept under nitrogen gas at 80 percent humidity, and the devices held up better in humid conditions than dry ones. Devices from separate batches behaved alike but not identically.

The team showed single devices and one connected pair, not a network trained to do a task. The authors wrote that practical use will take progress on the materials, the device design and the training methods.

Spector said the material could also suit devices that work with the body, such as prosthetics that process touch quickly or low-power health patches worn on the skin. The team also mentioned robots and environmental sensors.

Next, the team wants to build sensing into the same material, so a single squeezable layer can sense, remember and compute.

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances.

#6365. Scientists figured out how to use a cheap everyday camera to measure how well solar panels work

New digital tools turn massive amounts of complex data into simple, actionable insights to help leaders make better conservation decisions.

Solar panels glow if you run electricity into them in the dark. While photos easily show the bright and dim patches, measuring the exact brightness used to require an expensive, manually calibrated industrial camera.

Jürgen Werner and her research team from the University of Stuttgart, the Research Center Jülich, and the German company Solarzentrum Stuttgart got the same kind of number out of a $450 consumer camera, after writing down how its own electronics respond to light.

The camera is the easy part. A model of how it converts light into numbers is what makes the reading possible, and that model still leans on one reference cell with a known quality.

Push current into a solar cell and it behaves like an LED, giving off light of its own. Silicon cells glow in the infrared range, which the eye can’t see, so the picture has to come from a camera that can.

Engineers already use those pictures to check solar panels for cracked cells and broken connections. What they read is contrast. Bright areas are doing their job, dark ones aren’t.

The brightness itself is a measurement. The fraction of electrons that leave a solar cell as light instead of heat is its luminescent quantum efficiency.

The cell’s open-circuit voltage – the voltage it holds when nothing draws power from it – determines that fraction. Every tenfold rise adds about 60 mV to that voltage.

“An electroluminescence image contains much more quantitative information than simply showing bright and dark regions,” said Werner, of the Institute for Photovoltaics at the University of Stuttgart.

“With a suitable physical camera model and calibration, it can provide absolute luminescent quantum efficiency and, therefore, information about the local quality of a solar cell or module.”

Werner worked with Georgette Udo at Forschungszentrum Jülich and Liviu Stoicescu at Solarzentrum Stuttgart, a German company that inspects photovoltaic systems. Their camera was a Canon EOS 4000D, a low-cost model selling for around €400 in 2026.

Most consumer cameras carry a film over the sensor that absorbs infrared light, so the team took that film out. Astronomy hobbyists make the same change to shoot the night sky.

Then they screwed a long-pass filter onto the lens, which blocks the visible light that would otherwise wash out the faint glow.

The researchers took every photograph in the dark. A current source pushed a known current through each module, and the shutter time, the aperture and the ISO setting decided how much glow reached the sensor.

Brightness was then averaged across a whole cell in ImageJ, free image software, by drawing a box over the cell by hand.

Here is the problem that the model had to solve. A camera doesn’t report light honestly all the way up.

Below a certain brightness the number a pixel returns rises in step with the light that hits it, but above it the pixel fills up and the response stops rising.

That is over-exposure, familiar from any photograph taken into the sun.

Werner’s team measured where their own camera crossed over. It stayed linear below a brightness value of 400, and above that it bent toward a ceiling, which for one module sat at 1,177.

Both stretches are usable once the shape of the curve is known, and the saturated one yields a second estimate of the same quantity.

Converting brightness into quantum efficiency needs an anchor. The team took theirs from a cell with an established efficiency – 1.6 percent at 738 mV – and scaled everything else against it.

Eight silicon modules went under the camera, picked to span decades of production. The oldest was a Solarex panel built in 1978, with a module efficiency of 5.7 percent. At the other end, a Trina module from 2022 reached 21.1 percent.

A modern cell turns far more of its current into light, and by that measure a better cell is simply a brighter one.

Cells in the old panel averaged 560 mV of open-circuit voltage and a luminescent quantum efficiency of 0.0007 percent. Cells in the newer module ran at 687 mV and 0.23 percent.

Across those 45 years the quantum efficiency climbed by roughly a factor of 300.

The model had to fit both ends of that span of solar power manufacturing, and it mostly did. Readings landed where the 60 mV rule predicts, apart from four modules built with multicrystalline solar cells, which trap light less well than single-crystal ones.

Those four only fell into line after the team accounted for the difference.

Werner’s team didn’t put the camera up against an industrial one. The claim is narrower. A model of how a camera turns photons into numbers lets an ordinary one produce absolute values.

The weak points are the ones the authors name themselves. A box drawn by hand over each cell picks up the dark gaps between them, which put scatter in the data. An automatic version still has to be written.

Every measurement was made in the dark, on silicon, on modules whose performance was already known. And the whole scale depends on that single reference cell.

So far the authors haven’t pointed the calibrated camera at a module nobody has measured. That test would show whether the method grades hardware or only confirms what was known.

“Our next step is to use the calibrated camera to determine quantum efficiencies and open-circuit voltages of further, previously uncharacterized solar cells and modules,” Werner said.

He added that the same model should work on a panel lit up rather than powered up, and possibly outdoors.

Daylight matters most. The method needs a dark room, which keeps it in a laboratory. Outdoors, the camera could be carried along a row of panels at a working solar farm.

The full study was published in The Journal of Applied Physics.

#6364. Record-low temperature created on China’s space station

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

A Bose-Einstein condensate reached about 10 trillionths of a kelvin

An experiment on China's Tiangong space station (rendering shown) reached a record-low temperature in a state of matter called a Bose-Einstein condensate.

Shujianyang/Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Science has reached a new low. Temperature, that is.

Scientists cooled a collection of atoms to about 10 picokelvins, or 10 trillionths of a kelvin. That’s barely a smidge above absolute zero (−273.15° Celsius). The atoms formed a Bose-Einstein condensate, a quantum state of matter, colder than any before, researchers report November 5 in Science.

To achieve that record-low chill, scientists took their work to space. The atoms orbited Earth aboard China’s Tiangong space station. There, researchers used laser-based traps to contain 20,000 rubidium atoms and reduce their motion, thereby cooling them. At an atomic level, temperature is tied to motion: Atoms and molecules in the air around us move more slowly when it’s colder. Similarly, in systems of cold atoms, scientists can define an effective temperature based on how slowly the atoms spread apart when they are allowed to expand.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

On Earth, gravitational forces cause clouds of atoms to sag, reducing the effectiveness of cooling. But on the space station, the atoms experienced microgravity, the apparent weightlessness of an object in free fall.

To make a Bose-Einstein condensate, a disorderly gaggle of atoms is cooled until the atoms all take on the same quantum state, acting as one entity. By experimenting with ultracold atoms, researchers can study exotic states of matter and other mysterious physics. And they can test fundamental concepts, such as the equivalence principle — the idea that explains why objects of different masses fall at the same rate in a vacuum.

Spacefaring Bose-Einstein condensates were previously made on the International Space Station, at effective temperatures as low as 52 picokelvins. And an experiment on Earth, in which atoms were dropped down a tower to induce weightlessness, reached 38 picokelvins. But drop tower experiments are limited by the time their free fall lasts. That’s not an issue for experiments in Earth’s orbit. So cold atoms in space are really taking off.

Researchers found extreme levels of mercury in sediment cores in Mexico ‪—‬ and it’s all because the Maya loved red paint.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Maya used so much red paint that they accidentally poisoned their lakes and waterways with mercury, a new study finds.

The problem was cinnabar, a vivid-red mercury-sulfide mineral that can be used as the pigment vermilion in red paint. The run-off from the paint can enter waterways, where anaerobic bacteria then transform cinnabar into highly toxic methylmercury in the sediments of lakes. Over time, the methylmercury accumulates to higher levels in the food chain.

The ancient Maya, a people who lived in what is now southern Mexico and Central America and whose descendants are still around today, painted almost everything red. Archaeologists have found countless artifacts that the Maya reddened, including sculptures, monuments, walls, plazas, pottery and the dead for ceremonial funerals. Cinnabar was a common pigment in the paint they made, along with red ocher, which gets its color from a nontoxic iron mineral called hematite.

But the Maya passion for the color red — which to them represented the sun, blood and life — caused an environmental disaster when the nearby waters were poisoned by the cinnabar runoff, said study first author Matthew Waters, a paleolimnologist (a scientist who studies ancient waterways) at Auburn University in Alabama.

"They would have seen a strange color change in the water … and a drop in its productivity, such as fish for protein," he told Live Science. The Maya depended heavily on freshwater fisheries, including for freshwater shellfish.

Previous studies had already found evidence for high levels of mercury in the Maya's southern highlands and south-central lowlands, but no one had fully examined levels of the toxic mineral in Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula.

To investigate, Waters and his colleagues studied mercury levels in Maya-era mud in the Yucatán, and found overwhelming signs of mercury poisoning, probably from cinnabar paint, they reported in their study, published Nov. 4 in the journal Science Advances.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"We did not suspect [the Maya] used it in the quantities that we were seeing," he said.

The study found extreme levels of mercury in sediment cores from two Maya-era sites: Cobá Lake, a shallow lake beside the Maya city of that name, and Cenote Xcach (also spelled X-Canché), a flooded sinkhole beside a ruined city in the jungle that few have excavated.

The sediment cores chronicle the composition of earth and water over more than 2,000 years, and the times of mercury poisoning coincide with several periods during the Preclassic and Classic periods of the Maya civilization from about A.D. 40 to 820.

Waters explained that the Environmental Protection Agency in the U.S. has determined it is unsafe to drink water with mercury levels above 2 parts per billion, while the official limit for the level of mercury in fish, where it builds up over time, is 1 part per million — any number above that means the fish can be seized by authorities.

Severe poisoning occurs when the mercury levels in human blood exceed about 100 parts per billion, from drinking contaminated water or eating contaminated marine animals, such as fish. In humans, mercury poisoning can cause severe symptoms, including permanent lung damage, brain damage and death.

The reddish hue of the Maya sun god Kinich Ahau, made between the sixth and ninth centuries, now housed in Mexico’s National Museum of Anthropology, shows the Maya's love for mercury.

The most polluted parts of the Yucatan cores had a mercury level of 2.3 parts per million, the team discovered. "They experienced this for decades and, in one case, for centuries," Waters said.

The researchers then examined the sediment cores for signs of environmental damage caused by the mercury poisoning. They found that the cores lacked tiny fossils of freshwater shellfish, indicating that the high mercury levels were killing marine life. The team also noticed that the sediment cores had hardly any traces of algal blooms, which should have happened frequently, Waters said. That's likely because algae could not survive in the poisoned water nutrients.

Scholars debate why the Maya civilization collapsed in the eighth and ninth centuries, but a leading suspect is the disruption of food supplies caused by drought.

But although mercury levels were high during the Preclassic and Classic periods, the environmental damage caused by mercury levels had been falling in many places for hundreds of years by the time of the Maya collapse, Waters said, although it may have been a contributing factor.

Cinnabar does not occur naturally in the Yucatán, so it must have been imported there, probably from what's now Honduras, the researchers said. It seems these cinnabar imports eventually stopped at Cobá Lake, and the poisoning there fell to a background level of about 20 parts per billion by A.D. 520. However, the sediment cores showed that the mercury poisoning continued at Cenote Xcach until the collapse, they said.

Waters, M. N., Wooten, S. L., Abrook, A. M., Brenner, M., Curtis, J. H., Langdon, P. G., Medina-Gonzalez, R. M., Paradeisis-Stathis, S., & Vachula, R. S. (2026). Toxic mercury, aquatic ecosystem collapse, and the ancient Lowland Maya. Science Advances, 12(45), eaeh3280. https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aeh3280

#6361. Researchers found a way to grow full size broccoli under solar panels while making electricity at the same time

Under magenta solar panels passing a fraction of the sunlight, broccoli reached full head weight 25 days late while the panels made power.

Placing solar panels over a garden blocks the sun. That normally harms plant growth since most crops require plenty of light. However, that has proven not to be the case under all circumstances.

A new study shows that growing broccoli under special pink solar panels actually helps the plants use sunlight more efficiently.

While it took the broccoli an extra 25 days to mature, they still grew to full size because the semi-transparent panels were designed to let through the best red and blue light for growing.

This setup could allow farmers to harvest both crops and renewable energy from the exact same field.

Silvia Ma Lu of Mälardalen University in Västerås, Sweden, led the work. Her co-authors came from the same University and from two Italian institutes, the Institute for Sustainable Plant Protection in Florence and Università Cattolica in Piacenza.

“The basic concept is quite straightforward,” Ma Lu said. “The solar panels use part of the incoming sunlight to generate renewable electricity while allowing part of the light to pass through to the crops growing underneath.”

A leaf absorbs blue and red light and reflects more of the green, which is why plants look green. A magenta filter does the opposite, passing red and blue and blocking green.

So a magenta solar panel lets through the colors that a crop, such as broccoli, uses and absorbs the rest to make power.

Each panel is a sheet of glass with thin strips of a light-absorbing material, cadmium telluride, spaced across it. A magenta plastic layer inside the glass tints the light that passes between the strips.

Growing crops under panels is called agrivoltaics, and most projects use dark solar panels that cast heavy shade.

Ma Lu’s team built two canopies, each about 13 by 16 feet (4 by 5 meters) and 5 feet (1.5 meters) tall at the low edge.

One used panels the maker rates as 50 percent transparent, the other 70 percent. Under them, broccoli received about 13 and 19 percent, respectively, of the growing light that reached a third, open plot.

Seedlings went into all three plots at Kärrbo Prästgård, a farm in central Sweden, on July 2, 2024. There were thus 44 plants per plot, under white insect netting.

The open-field broccoli was ready to cut after 79 days. At that point the plants growing under the panels were shorter, with smaller heads and thinner stems, so the team let them keep growing.

By day 104, the heads under both canopies weighed about the same as the open-field heads had at day 79. Whole plants in the open still weighed more.

The shaded plants had grown 25 to 41 percent more leaves than their neighbors in the sun. No plant in any plot developed a hollow stem, a defect that the team checked for.

A later harvest could also land in weeks when fresh broccoli sells for more, the authors noted.

Full sun at midday delivered about 925 units of growing light to the open plot, counted as photons per square meter per second.

The canopies passed 143 and 207 of those units, yet the shaded broccoli produced nearly as much plant matter. Each unit of light yielded up to 4.5 times more dry weight than it did in the open.

Single leaves showed the same pattern under a lamp. Leaves from under the panels photosynthesized faster at every light level than leaves from the open plot.

On sunny days the open-field plants were likely getting more light than they could use, Ma Lu’s team wrote. The shaded plants had adjusted to capture more of the little light they did get.

Afternoons under the panels were about 1.8°F (1.0°C) warmer than in the open plot, and nights about 2°F (1.1°C) cooler. The air was also about 6 percent more humid, so the shaded plants lost less water.

Rain was plentiful from September on and, with drip irrigation before that, soil moisture was not what limited either plot.

At the first sampling, iron in the shaded heads was 37 to 41 percent lower than in open-field heads, and manganese was 38 to 42 percent lower. Zinc was down 18 to 20 percent, copper 12 percent, and dissolved sugars by a third to a half.

Calcium, magnesium, and potassium rose instead, 25 to 54 percent higher under the panels in September. By the second harvest those three had fallen back to match the open-field heads, while the four trace metals stayed low.

“One of the most interesting findings was how similarly the broccoli performed under the two solar panel systems despite their different transparency levels,” Ma Lu said.

“However, these findings are specific to our experimental conditions and should be validated across additional growing seasons and system configurations.”

The denser canopy generated an estimated 447.6 kilowatt hours over the season from panels rated at 1.1 kilowatts, converting 7.2 percent of the sunlight hitting them to electricity. Standard silicon panels convert 20 percent or more.

On paper, the team also scaled the numbers up. By that estimate, 2.5 acres (1 hectare) under these panels would produce as much food and power as 2.9 acres (1.18 hectares) split between a field and a solar farm.

“Configurations similar to our prototype may currently be suitable for smaller-scale applications, such as community gardens, or for integration into greenhouse roofs rather than immediate deployment over large agricultural areas,” Ma Lu said.

Each treatment had one plot, six sampled plants, and a single season in central Sweden behind it. Plants at the canopy edges got extra sun and may have shaded or sheltered the ones measured in the middle.

In the 25 days after the open-field harvest, those plants could have grown side shoots for a second cut that the study did not weigh.

The study also can’t separate the magenta color from plain shade or from the softer, scattered light under glass.

Ma Lu’s team has begun testing the magenta panels, along with red and blue ones, under lab lighting where no outside light leaks in.

The full study was published in the journal Cell Reports Physical Science.

#6359. Corn fights back against a fungus – but its defense has a hidden weakness

A corn smut fungus uses the plant’s own defense enzymes to release a hidden signal that activates a receptor and speeds fungal cell division.

Corn, like every plant, fights back when something breaks in. When a fungus pushes into its tissue, the plant sends out enzymes that chop up proteins, including the ones the intruder secretes.

For the fungus behind corn smut, that defense turns out to be exactly the signal it has been waiting for.

The plant’s enzymes cut a protein secreted by the fungus, releasing a signal that helps the invader detect that it has entered plant tissue.

That cut frees a short fragment that was folded away inside. The fragment switches on a receptor in the fungal cell membrane, and the fungus starts dividing faster.

The plant’s defense, in other words, tells the invader it has arrived.

Florian Altegoer, who leads a research group at the Institute of Microbiology at Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf, led the work with lead author Gabriel Mendoza-Rojas, a member of his group.

Colleagues at the University of Göttingen, NC State University, Imperial College London, and the University of Groningen took part.

The receptor belongs to a family of proteins called G protein-coupled receptors, which work as sensors in a cell’s outer membrane and relay signals from outside to inside.

Humans have more than 800 of them, and they are the targets of about 40% of approved drugs. Fungal versions are far less understood.

“We have identified a previously unknown fungal GPCR and uncovered an unusual mechanism by which it is activated,” Altegoer said.

Mendoza-Rojas put the twist more bluntly.

“The fungus thus ironically utilizes enzymes from its host plant to detect that it has entered the tissue successfully,” he said.

The fungus, Ustilago maydis, infects maize plants and causes large galls, especially on the ears, where it makes its spores.

Two of its genes were already known to be essential: delete either one and the fungus produces almost no galls.

One of those genes makes a secreted protein called Pit2, which corn enzymes cut into a fragment that blocks those same enzymes.

The other made a membrane protein of unknown function. When the team searched the fungal genome for proteins with the seven-helix shape of a receptor, that protein was one of 34 hits. They renamed it Gpe1.

They put the receptor into baker’s yeast engineered to glow red whenever it fires. Intact Pit2 produced a weak glow. Fragments of Pit2 fully activated the reporter at a tenth of the dose.

The team narrowed the active fragment down to nine amino acids.

The team also grew crystals of Pit2 and mapped its shape, which helped explain why the intact protein activates the receptor only weakly.

Two copies lock together, and the nine-amino-acid stretch is buried in the seam between them. Only the plant’s enzymes can release it.

“The peptide is hidden inside Pit2, like treasure in a chest that only plant enzymes can open,” Mendoza-Rojas said.

“However, opening this chest is more like opening Pandora’s box: It releases a signal that benefits the fungus at the plant’s expense.”

The team then watched living fungal cells under a microscope while the fragment flowed past them.

Soon after, the receptor pulled back from the cell surface into the cell’s interior, a common response of a receptor that has been triggered.

The cells also budded sooner. One round of division took about 226 minutes without the fragment and about 167 minutes with it, close to an hour less.

Faster division fits what the fungus has to do. It pauses its cell cycle while it grows a thread into the plant, then restarts division once it’s inside.

A regulator called Clp1 is part of that restart. Cells carrying extra Gpe1 made about five times as much of the Clp1 gene’s messenger molecule, and the fragment pushed it higher still.

“Our work establishes a mechanistic link between sensing the host environment and resuming fungal proliferation after entry,” Altegoer said.

The receptor mattered in whole plants too. The team changed single building blocks in the receptor’s predicted binding pocket and infected corn seedlings with the altered fungi.

Two of the changes, which also crippled the receptor in yeast, sharply reduced the galls on seedlings scored 12 days later.

Gpe1 has relatives across the smut fungi, but Pit2 shows up only in the corn fungus’s close relatives. The team tested whether each receptor would respond to the other species’ signal.

The signal from a related corn fungus switched on the corn smut receptor. The signal from a barley smut did not, and the corn fragments only weakly activated the barley receptor.

The nine-amino-acid stretch itself has barely changed across those species, which the authors read as the receptor and its signal evolving together.

A structural search also turned up a broad family of related receptors across the fungal group that includes mushrooms and smuts.

One patch of Gpe1 resembles a switch found in a large class of human receptors, including the light sensor in the eye.

The picture of how the fragment sits in the receptor comes from a computer prediction, which the team used only to decide which parts of the protein to alter.

The two weakest receptor variants might also be less stable rather than worse at binding, and the authors wrote that they can’t yet separate those explanations.

The restart of cell division is also only partly explained. The increase in Clp1 messenger RNA after receptor activation offers a possible explanation.

And the plant’s enzymes cut Pit2 into more than one fragment. One blocks the plant’s defenses; the other switches on the receptor.

How much each contributes during a real infection has not been tested, and that is the next experiment the authors wrote has to be done.

Whether other fungi that infect crops use the same mechanism is the larger open question, and the team plans to look.

“We want to find out whether other fungi use comparable receptors to sense their surroundings and adjust their growth,” Altegoer said.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Communications.

#6358. When would aliens contact Earth? Astronomers test a new idea

Astronomers are searching for alien signals at a moving point opposite the Sun, testing a strategy that could help distant civilizations make contact.

Searching for alien signals sounds like a question of which star to aim a telescope at. It’s also a question of when to listen, because a civilization sending a focused radio beam toward Earth might transmit only at selected times.

For the first time, astronomers have specifically searched a moving point in the sky that could offer a shared cue for when to transmit and listen. They found no evidence of extraterrestrial technology.

Sofia Sheikh of the SETI Institute and Eleanor Hort of the University of New Mexico led the search, which used the Allen Telescope Array in Hat Creek, California.

Three nights of pilot observations in the summer of 2023 turned up 1.9 million radio signals, and all of them could be explained by human technology.

Two people who agree to meet in a city but forget to pick a time and place still have a decent chance of finding each other.

Each one picks the landmark the other is most likely to pick. Game theorists call that shared choice a Schelling point.

The team applied the same logic to a distant transmitter. From some directions in the galaxy, an observer would see Earth cross the face of the Sun once a year.

That crossing tells them a planet exists and how long its year is. It also shows the planet orbits at a distance where water can stay liquid.

Halfway through the crossing, Earth lies exactly between the transmitter and the Sun.

Seen from Earth, the transmitter would be in the direction directly opposite the Sun, a spot astronomers call the anti-solar point.

A sender could beam a signal toward Earth at that alignment, while astronomers on Earth listened toward the anti-solar point, without either side arranging contact beforehand.

“The challenge in SETI isn’t simply deciding where to point a telescope,” Sheikh said. “It’s figuring out where and when another civilization might choose to transmit.”

The idea is not new: a 1982 paper proposed it for Jupiter’s crossings, and a 2003 paper argued Earth’s were the better bet.

Yet by 2020, the Breakthrough Listen archive held not a single pointing within half a degree of the anti-solar point.

Two large radio surveys of the 1990s likely spent about 0.0004% of their time there, by accident.

The spot never stays put. As Earth moves around the Sun, the anti-solar point slides along the sky against the background stars, so the telescope has to follow it night after night.

The survey plans repeated observations two to three nights a week over about four years to build coverage along Earth’s orbit.

For the pilot, the team pointed 20 of the array’s 42 dishes at the anti-solar point for about 17 hours over three nights. The scans ran five minutes each and added up to 32 terabytes of data.

They listened between 1.06 and 2.38 gigahertz, a band that includes the radio frequency of hydrogen that early searchers once favored.

Every scan also recorded a second patch of sky nearby.

A signal from a distant point source should show up strongly in the target beam and faintly in the other. Interference from a satellite or a phone tower tends to appear in both.

The two-beam comparison alone removed 1.3 million of the 1.9 million signals. The team then plotted the most promising 2,114 and inspected each one by eye.

None of them looked like a deliberate alien signal.

Most were narrow and barely shifting in frequency, the signature of ground-based transmitters, and the few that drifted lined up with known sources of human interference, including satellite links.

A search that finds nothing still says something, because the old Arecibo planetary radar sent out a tight beam with an effective power of roughly 20 trillion watts.

The pilot was sensitive enough to catch a transmitter that strong from 44 to 124 light-years away.

The exact reach depends on where the signal fell in the beam and how fast its frequency drifted.

The pilot sets the first limit of any kind on alien signals timed to the anti-solar point. The limit applies to a narrow strip, though.

The telescope’s beam spans only about 5% of the width of the zone from which Earth’s crossings are visible. A transmitter slightly above or below that line would have been missed.

The full survey began after the pilot, two to three nights a week at higher frequencies chosen to dodge the worst interference. It has already logged more than 121 nights.

The team plans to report the first year of data in a later paper.

A detection would need a lot to be true: a civilization within reach, one that has noticed Earth, and one that reasons about meeting points the way people do.

The team doesn’t assume any of that; the search is a way to test it. It also assumes the sender has accounted for how long light takes to cross the gap, so the signal arrives when Earth expects it.

Whether anyone is transmitting at the anti-solar point is still an open question, and three nights can’t settle it.

The multiyear survey will test the idea across a much broader stretch of sky.

The full study was published in the journal The Astronomical Journal.

#6357. How octopuses squeeze through tiny openings, step by step

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The cephalopod how-to guide involves three or four moves, depending on a hole’s size

Octopuses are famous for fleeing tanks by squeezing through narrow slits and impossibly tiny holes. Now scientists have studied the sequences some cephalopods like this Mayan octopus use to make such great escapes.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Octopuses have made many a great escape. Remember Inky, who fled from New Zealand’s national aquarium?

The cephalopods can Houdini their way out of tanks and off boats by squeezing through narrow slits and incredibly tiny holes. Now researchers know exactly how some octopuses pull it off. These masterful getaways involve a consistent, step-by-step game plan, researchers report November 5 in the Journal of Experimental Biology.

Octopuses are mostly squishy muscle, allowing them to shape-shift, though they do have some rigid body parts. Not many scientists have studied how these animals squirm through small openings, says Robyn Crook, an evolutionary biologist at San Francisco State University who was not involved in the research. “It’s one of the most characteristic behaviors of octopuses in popular awareness, but the strategies octopuses use have not really been examined systematically.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Sneaking through small spaces isn’t just a party trick for octopuses, says Michael Kuba, a biologist at the University of Naples Federico II in Italy. The animals use that skill to find hidden food and to avoid becoming food themselves.

Kuba and his colleagues observed how three common octopuses (Octopus vulgaris) and four Mayan octopuses (Octopus maya) approached small holes. For each individual, the team measured the distance between the octopus’s eyes as an indicator of the size of their most rigid cartilage around their brain. Then the researchers designed acrylic boxes with holes that were slightly smaller or larger than that eye-to-eye measurement. They plopped the octopuses inside and watched what happened.

Octopuses have slightly different escape how-tos, depending on the size of the hole they are squeezing through. Here, a common octopus (Octopus vulgaris) wriggles through a space just a little bit bigger than their most rigid body parts. It takes just three steps for the octopus to free itself from the acrylic box.

W. Xin et al/J. of Experimental Biology 2026, reproduced with permission of The Company of Biologists

Common octopuses used one of two escape strategies depending on the hole’s size. When the hole was wider than the distance between their eyes, the octopuses pushed themselves through it in three steps. First, they snuck one or two arms through the hole and then threaded a couple more arms through. Finally, they used the arms that they had already snaked through the hole to push against the box and yank their head and the rest of their arms through in one fell swoop. The whole operation took a few seconds.

When the hole was narrower, common octopuses added a fourth step. They shoved all of their arms through the hole first and then squished their head and bulbous mantle through.

When a hole is smaller than their most rigid body parts, common octopuses add a fourth step to wrestle their bodies through an opening.

W. Xin et al/J. of Experimental Biology 2026, reproduced with permission of The Company of Biologists

Mayan octopuses behaved more cautiously than the common octopuses. When confronted with the narrower hole, Mayan octopuses didn’t even attempt to fit inside of it. They usually ignored it. This difference between the species could stem from their biology or how they’ve adapted to their environments, Kuba says. Mayan octopuses live in sandy, rocky areas, so while they might disappear under rocks, they don’t often need to cram through holes, he says.

The team hopes these escape artists will inspire new soft robots that can morph their shape to fit through tiny spaces, says Wenci Xin, a robotics researcher at the National University of Singapore. “This incredible capability could enable robots to overcome environmental limitations and enter spaces that are difficult to reach.”

Studying how octopuses navigate different types of holes may provide additional clues for robots, Crook says. For instance, the cephalopods may take a different tack for openings that are more like slits or tubes than holes.

Currently, robots built to fit through tiny holes tend to be snake-shaped, but further research on these eight-armed contortionists could unlock other configurations.

The Vikings are famous for being warriors, but how often did Viking women take part in battles?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Vikings were explorers, farmers, merchants and, most famously, warriors who launched raids across large parts of Europe.

Stereotypes of Vikings usually conjure up images of muscular men. But over the past few decades, researchers have turned their attention to women of the Viking Age (roughly A.D. 793 to 1066) and the roles they held. For instance, there are stories of "shield maidens" who fought alongside men, and some of these texts mention Viking women who fought in battle. The archaeological record also holds evidence, including graves of Viking Age women who were buried with war-grade weapons and shields.

It's still a matter of debate whether women who lived during the Viking Age could be warriors, but this discussion raises another question: It's one thing to have texts describing female fighters and archaeological records of women buried with weapons, but what can the evidence tell us about how frequently Viking women fought in battle?

The answer, experts told Live Science, largely depends on our interpretation of texts, artifacts, and burials of Viking Age women, which often face higher scrutiny than burials of men who were buried with similar (or even fewer) weapons.

The Vikings used a runic system of writing, but they left precious few texts behind. Instead, much of what we know about the Vikings was written about them by people from other cultures or by their Norse descendants.

One of the most evocative texts was written in the 12th century by the Danish historian and theologian Saxo Grammaticus. In "Gesta Danorum" (Latin for "History of the Danes" and translated by Jenny Jochens), he wrote that "there were once women in Denmark who dressed themselves to look like men and spent almost every minute cultivating [combat] skills." As "if they were forgetful of their true selves they put toughness before allure, aimed at conflicts instead of kisses, tasted blood, not lips, sought the clash of arms rather than the arm's embrace, fitted to weapons hands what should have been weaving, desired not the couch but the kill, and those they could have appeased with looks they attacked with lances."

Another text about the Vikings, the medieval Irish "Cogadh Gaedhelre Gallaibh" ("War of the Irish with the Foreigners"), refers to a woman known as the "Red Lady" leading a Viking fleet in a raid on Belfast in the 10th century.

Feed your curiosity with an exclusive mystery every week, solved with science and delivered direct to your inbox before it's seen anywhere else.

There's a lot of uncertainty, said Neil Price, an archaeology professor at Uppsala University in Sweden who has written extensively about the Vikings. The text in the "Cogadh Gaedhel re Gallaibh" that refers to the Red Lady is of debatable accuracy, Price told Live Science in an email.

He suspects that Viking women fought in battle but not frequently. In addition, "female warriors were probably a very small minority," Price said.

A modern-day reenactment depicting Viking warriors.

The account written by Saxo Grammaticus is also contentious. Thomas Kristian Heebøll-Holm, a history professor at the University of Southern Denmark, said Saxo Grammaticus is not a reliable source.

"Saxo Grammaticus does write about female warriors, but only in the parts of his work concerned [with] the legendary past of Denmark," Heebøll-Holm told Live Science in an email. "Furthermore, these writings are not accurate, but moral and fictitious," Heebøll-Holm said, noting that, in some instances, Saxo Grammaticus seemed to be drawing on the stories of the Amazons, a group of legendary female warriors whom the ancient Greeks believed in with stories about them dating back more than 2,500 years.

Archaeological evidence can also be challenging to interpret. Archaeologists know of about 30 Viking Age female burials containing weapons, including three with swords in Scandinavia. Even more Viking Age women's graves have items that could have been used as weapons ‪—‬ including spears, axes and knives ‪—‬ although these tools also could have been used for hunting or tending to farms. Either way, we can't be sure if these women fought in battle.

"The first concern is that the weapons were really used by the deceased and were not merely included as signs of special status or social rank acquired through inheritance," Deborah Shepherd, an independent researcher who holds a doctorate in archaeology and has studied the Vikings extensively, told Live Science in an email. She noted that graves are often not well preserved, making it difficult to gather information.

This 1889 illustration shows a grave at Birka in Sweden. It is now known that the person buried with war-grade weapons and riding gear is a woman.

There were likely "some few female warriors, but they were probably only found in the highest ranking families, and their warrior career was probably short-lived," Shepherd said. "They wouldn't have fought in the great armies of later centuries but possibly did fight in pre-Christian skirmishes." (The Vikings began gradually converting to Christianity between the ninth and 12th centuries.)

There is at least one known case of a Viking woman found with what may be combat-related injuries. A Viking woman found in Solør, Norway, had a head injury consistent with a sword strike. She was 18 or 19 at the time she died, was buried with weapons and lived around 900.

Ole Kastholm, a curator and senior researcher at the Roskilde Museum in Denmark, said there is a lot of uncertainty regarding how frequently Viking Age women fought in battle.

Weapons "do occur as a grave good in a handful of graves with female human remains," Kastholm told Live Science in an email. "Often it is just a single weapon [such] as a spear or [a] battle axe. But we know of at least one example of a female grave with a full set of weapons as well as riding equipment," which is located in Birka, Sweden.

"If this was a man's grave, researchers would have no doubt that it was a warrior grave, and this explanation must necessarily also apply when the interred is a woman," Kastholm said.

That said, there were female warriors in other cultures. "One can also note in passing that female warriors were an almost common feature of central Asian societies for at least a millennium before the Viking Age," Price wrote in his book, "The Sea-King and the Sorceress: Life and Death in the Viking Age" (Basic Books, 2026).

For instance the Scythians are a people who flourished in eastern Europe and Asia and Scythian women have been found buried with horses and weapons. In some cases, the Scythian women suffered combat wounds such as arrowheads and it's been speculated that they may have been an inspiration for stories of the Amazons.

See how much you know about ancient norsemen with our Viking quiz!

Owen Jarus is a regular contributor to Live Science who writes about archaeology and humans' past. He has also written for The Independent (UK), The Canadian Press (CP) and The Associated Press (AP), among others. Owen has a bachelor of arts degree from the University of Toronto and a journalism degree from Ryerson University.

#6354. Patients admit lying to get antibiotics – and most say it worked

A survey of 959 U.S. adults explores why some patients exaggerate or invent symptoms to obtain antibiotics, and how often they report success.

Many people walk into a clinic hoping to leave with antibiotics. In a new survey, more than a quarter of the American adults questioned said they had gone further.

To get antibiotics, they exaggerated how severe their symptoms were, said they had lasted longer than they had, or made up symptoms entirely.

Most of those who tried said it worked at least once.

Alistair Thorpe of University of Utah Health and Andrea Levy of CT State Community College led the survey, with Angela Fagerlin of Utah as the study’s senior author.

The 959 adults who answered came from an online survey panel rather than a random sample, and everything rests on what they admitted to. So the team called the numbers a first estimate rather than a national count.

“It is a tough situation,” Thorpe said. “People are experiencing unpleasant symptoms, and they can have this strong feeling that antibiotics are the only thing that can help them feel better.”

“Being told to just rest and wait is a hard thing to do, and if you think there’s something that could make you feel better, it’s a very hard impulse to override,” he added.

The survey asked two plain questions. Had the person ever told a health care provider that symptoms were worse or lasted longer than they did, in order to get antibiotics?

And had they ever claimed a symptom they didn’t have at all?

Of the 959 respondents, 268 said yes to at least one, and more than half of those had done both.

About one in four had stretched a real symptom, such as a cough reported as two weeks old when it was one week old.

About one in six had invented one, such as a fever that never happened.

Cold-like symptoms were the ones most often misrepresented, named by about two-thirds of the group. Stomach trouble and joint or muscle pain came next.

Of those 268 people, 206 said the tactic had earned them antibiotics at least once. Asked where they learned what to say, they most often named their own experience, then friends and family, then a clinician.

About one in five pointed to social media, and 31 said an AI chatbot had coached them.

Why do it? The reasons people ticked most often were plain. About 62% said they had felt really sick, and almost as many believed antibiotics were the only thing that would help.

About 61% wanted to get back to work or parenting faster, and 57% didn’t want to pass an illness to someone close to them.

Just over half said they knew their own body better than any provider. About 41% wanted spare antibiotics on hand for next time, and 40% saw no downside to taking them.

Antibiotics kill bacteria and do nothing against the viruses behind most colds and flu-like illnesses.

Every unneeded course also helps bacteria build resistance to the drugs, a problem researchers have traced from farm manure to the bacteria in human guts.

“These medications are not totally benign for the patient,” said Levy, a professor of social sciences. “And antibiotic use contributes to increasing antimicrobial resistance, which is a broader public health concern.”

Age mattered most. Adults under 56 had about three times the odds of reporting it as those 65 and older. Gender, race, and education were not linked to it.

Trust mattered too. People who often felt that clinicians didn’t take their symptoms seriously had about twice the odds of having misrepresented them.

People who endorsed at least one claim that antibiotic resistance is a hoax also had higher odds of reporting symptom misrepresentation.

Nearly a third of all respondents held such a belief, and one in five agreed that drug companies invented resistance to charge more.

Greater antibiotic knowledge was associated with lower odds of reporting symptom misrepresentation.

Those who said they needed help reading health materials had more than twice the odds.

Across the whole sample, 64% either thought antibiotics work on viruses or weren’t sure.

Thorpe said a past prescription can teach the wrong lesson. A viral infection clears on its own, and a person who was given antibiotics for one can credit the pills for the recovery.

Only 77 of the 268 said they regretted misrepresenting their symptoms, and 73 regretted taking the antibiotics they got.

The regrets people wrote in were more often about side effects or pills that didn’t help than about the lie itself.

Fewer than half said there was anyone they would listen to if told not to do it again.

The 691 respondents who said they had never done it gave their own reasons.

About 96% said honesty with a doctor matters so the doctor can treat them properly, 89% said they trust their clinician’s judgment, and 85% called lying morally wrong.

“There are very understandable reasons that we can sympathize with about why patients might feel the need to misrepresent symptoms, or why caregivers might do so on behalf of their children,” Levy said.

“We’re simply saying: perhaps there’s a better way.”

The panel was recruited with quotas for age, gender, race, and region, but people who sign up for paid online surveys are not a cross-section of the population.

The team said the figures should be read as a starting point for larger studies.

Self-reporting may have led to underestimates.

Some people may have hidden a lie, which would make the true share higher, and the question asked about “ever,” so faded memories may have cut it as well.

The survey also did not ask how often anyone did it or exactly what they said.

“Going forward, it will be important to test different ways to change the communication patterns between patients and their clinicians,” said Fagerlin, who chairs the Department of Population Health Sciences at Utah.

Future research could test whether helping patients feel heard encourages more honest conversations about symptoms and antibiotics.

The full study was published in the journal JAMA Network Open.

#6352. Can a bird flu vaccine keep up with a virus that keeps changing?

A computer-designed bird flu vaccine protected mice against three H5N1 strains, offering early evidence of broader protection before human trials.

Governments hold doses of bird flu vaccine in storage for the day the virus starts spreading between people.

Each of those vaccines was built around a single virus sample. H5 bird flu, meanwhile, keeps splitting into branches that look different to the immune system.

A Cambridge team built a rival vaccine, with active ingredients drawn up by computer instead of copied from one virus.

Researchers gave it to mice, then exposed separate groups to three H5N1 viruses spanning two decades of evolution.

Every one of those mice lived. Half the mice given the stockpile-style vaccine died after exposure to the clade 1 virus.

The study was led by Jonathan Heeney, a professor of research in vaccinology in the Department of Veterinary Medicine at the University of Cambridge.

The vaccine comes out of the university spin-out DIOSynVax, where he and several co-authors are employees or shareholders.

The tests were in mice and ferrets, and no one has given this vaccine to a person.

In an interview with Earth.com, Heeney said vaccine design has spent most of a century looking the wrong way.

“For more than 70 years, vaccines against rapidly evolving viruses have largely been designed by looking backwards at the pathogen that already exists,” he said.

Bird flu now turns up in wild birds, poultry and mammals on nearly every continent. The H5 family has broken into branches that evolve on their own in Asia, Europe, Africa and the Americas.

How dangerous those branches are varies sharply.

The clade 2.3.4.4b viruses spreading in the Americas have caused 97 known human cases and three deaths, and most of those infections were mild.

These viruses have also spread through dairy herds.

The 2.3.2.1e viruses circulating in Southeast Asia have killed more than half the people with reported infections over the past two years.

The bird flu vaccines in national stockpiles are matched to single virus samples, picked through the World Health Organization’s influenza program.

Those vaccines haven’t been widely tested against the other H5 branches now circulating, the authors wrote.

“These vaccines are based on single viral isolates, whereas H5Nx viruses have continued to evolve and diversify into multiple lineages around the world,” Heeney told Earth.com.

“In many cases, viral evolution has outpaced the strains on which those stockpiled vaccines were originally based.”

The part of a vaccine that teaches the immune system has a name: the antigen.

Rather than lift one from a single virus, the team pooled the genetic sequences of H5 viruses collected worldwide by surveillance programs.

Software then drew up antigens carrying the features shared across the whole group.

The vaccine carries mRNA instructions for making three designed antigens.

One is based on the outer protein the virus uses to get into a cell, and a second on the protein it uses to get back out.

The third is a small protein that helps rouse the immune response.

The team screened the candidates in cells, then packaged mRNA encoding the selected antigens inside tiny fat particles, using the same delivery approach as mRNA COVID-19 vaccines.

Heeney said the design looks ahead instead of back.

He noted that his platform uses computational biology to anticipate viral evolution and design broadly protective vaccine antigens before the next outbreak occurs.

The team immunized mice, then exposed them to H5N1 viruses from three branches that have all infected people: clade 1, clade 2.3.2.1e and clade 2.3.4.4b.

All mice given the designed vaccine survived exposure to their assigned H5N1 virus, with no weight loss or signs of illness.

Four days after exposure, no virus could be recovered from their lungs or spleens. The stockpile-style vaccine matched to 2.3.4.4b protected fully against its own matched virus.

Against the 2.3.2.1e virus, 67% of those mice survived, and against clade 1, 50% did.

Blood tests pointed the same way. Antibodies from the designed vaccine blocked lab-made stand-ins for eleven H5 branches.

Each stockpile-style vaccine covered only its own corner of the family.

Ferrets catch and spread flu much as people do, making them an important model for testing influenza vaccines.

The team exposed them to a 2.3.4.4b H5N1 taken from an Italian chicken. In the entry protein, it differs from the stockpile vaccine’s strain by four amino acids.

Every unvaccinated ferret died or reached the humane endpoint by day eight. So did half of those given the stockpile-style vaccine.

All ferrets given the lower dose of the designed vaccine survived without weight loss or fever. One ferret given the higher dose reached the humane endpoint.

The oddity sits in the bloodwork. On the day of exposure, those ferrets scored below the antibody level flu researchers treat as protective against that virus.

Most survived despite those low antibody readings.

Something other than that one measure was carrying the protection, the authors wrote, most likely antibodies against the exit protein working alongside antibodies against the entry protein.

The comparison is not clean, and the authors wrote as much.

Their vaccine is mRNA, while the benchmark is a killed whole virus, so dose, formulation and delivery all differ along with the antigen design.

Comparing both antigen designs using the same mRNA platform would help isolate the effect of antigen design.

The mice also got a single dose of the stockpile-style comparator, a benchmark taken from older work.

And the designed vaccine’s edge over the stockpile shots can’t yet be pinned on the antigen design alone.

Nobody has measured whether any of this holds in people.

The next steps are manufacturing the vaccine to meet regulatory standards and a first trial in humans, Heeney said, and DIOSynVax is raising money to pay for them.

The designed antigen sequences are patented.

What the virus does in the meantime is the part nobody controls. “It’s when bird flu adapts to live in the airways of mammals that we start to get really nervous,” Heeney said.

That is the shift researchers watch for in dairy cows and pigs, and the reason a bird flu vaccine that protects against multiple branches could be valuable.

The full study was published in the journal Cell Reports Medicine.

#6351. Water sinking near Antarctica carries nutrients on a decades-long journey

Southern Ocean nutrients ride north for decades in two sinking water layers, and a new study finds each layer recycles a different mix.

The Southern Ocean looks remote, about as far from the Gulf of Maine or the North Pacific as water gets. Yet the water that sinks there each winter spends decades sliding north beneath the world’s oceans.

It carries nutrients that support plankton growth across much of the ocean.

A new study finds that two of those sinking layers recycle their nutrients in different ways. Each one arrives decades later with a different mix.

Barney Balch, a senior research scientist emeritus at Bigelow Laboratory for Ocean Sciences in Maine, led the work.

He collaborated with colleagues at the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution, the Bermuda Institute of Ocean Sciences, Texas A&M University and the University of Miami.

The team sampled water from a ship along a single line south of Hawaii, so the findings describe one slice of the Pacific.

“When you integrate this water around the globe, the nutrient regeneration in Subantarctic Mode Water and Antarctic Intermediate Water supports about three-quarters of the primary production on Earth north of the 30th parallel south,” Balch said.

Powerful winds and currents pull deep water up to the surface around Antarctica.

Winter cooling mixes it into thick, uniform layers, and some of that water sinks again and heads north.

Two layers matter here. Subantarctic Mode Water forms farther north and rides higher.

Antarctic Intermediate Water forms closer to the ice, slides beneath the mode water, and ends up 2,000 to 3,600 feet (600 to 1,100 meters) down.

Both layers carry the remains of dead plankton sinking from above. Microbes break those remains down, and nitrogen and phosphorus return to the water in forms plankton can use again.

The glass-like shells of diatoms dissolve more slowly and release silicate, which diatoms need to build new shells.

The research vessel Roger Revelle left Honolulu on December 26, 2020. It worked its way south along the 150th meridian west to 60 degrees south and returned in February 2021.

The hard part was knowing how old each parcel of water was.

The team used chlorofluorocarbons, the refrigerant gases that leaked into the air through much of the 20th century.

The mix of those gases changed year by year as factories switched compounds, so water that last touched the air carries a blend that can be matched to a year.

By that clock, the mode water was mostly 35 to 40 years old.

The intermediate water ran older, up to about 70 years. Pairing the ages with nutrient levels let the team turn a snapshot into rates of change.

“What makes this paper unique is that we are combining the biological or chemical measurements with the time clock, the CFC-derived age of the water, which allows you to talk about rates,” Balch said.

In the mode water, nitrate built up about seven times faster than in the intermediate water, and phosphate about six times faster.

Both are essential, and nitrogen often limits how much plankton can grow, so the shallower layer is the one getting richer on its journey.

The mode water also gained dissolved carbon about twice as fast, and it appeared to use up oxygen faster too, which fits more microbial activity there.

The team wrote that mixing with neighboring water can inflate rates like these, by as much as double.

Silicate was the exception. It accumulated almost twice as fast in the deeper intermediate water as in the mode water, at about 2.6 against 1.4 micromoles per kilogram of seawater per year.

The split could matter at the surface. When the mode water finally mixes back up into sunlit water, its nitrogen-rich recipe would favor plankton that don’t need silica.

One example is the coccolithophores, which armor themselves in chalk plates.

Deeper, stronger mixing that brings up intermediate water would favor diatoms, the glass-shelled algae of cold waters.

One result surprised the authors. Silicate accumulated in the intermediate water at least 20 times faster than the slow dissolution of suspended shells could explain.

That points to fast-sinking clumps of diatom debris as a major source.

Temperature and salinity shifted with age too. In the mode water, the youngest samples were warmer and saltier than the oldest.

Across the samples, temperature decreased by about 0.3°C for each additional year of estimated water age.

This relationship was much steeper than warming trends reported in other Southern Ocean records.

In the intermediate water, the youngest water was fresher, the opposite trend.

The authors wrote that those patterns could record changing conditions where the layers form, or mixing with water above and below along the way. The data can’t tell which.

Older samples also occurred at greater depths, with each additional year of estimated age corresponding to about 240 feet (73 meters) in the mode water and 128 feet (39 meters) in the intermediate water.

The study covers one north-south line in one season, and the chlorofluorocarbon clock itself is uncertain by roughly 30%.

The authors wrote that they could not fully separate recycling inside each layer from year-to-year changes in the water when it formed, or from mixing along the way.

Whether the two recipes actually change which plankton bloom when the water resurfaces, decades after it sank, has not been measured.

The test would be to follow the same layers into the North Pacific, where they finally return to the light.

The full study was published in the journal Journal of Geophysical Research: Oceans.

NASA's Swift Observatory went out in a blaze of glory this week, but it left behind millions of images of the universe that could fuel discoveries for decades.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Early Wednesday (Nov. 4), NASA's Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory fell out of space, burning up in the sky over Sumatra. It was a fitting, fiery end for a telescope that spent 22 years studying the most powerful explosions in the universe — and, even with Swift gone, its observations will continue to feed scientific curiosity for years to come.

Swift's most important contributions to astronomy are not exactly eye candy. Designed to swivel toward deep-space explosions at a moment's notice, Swift excelled at capturing bright, fleeting and faraway specks of light. The multiwavelength observatory was equipped with optical, ultraviolet (UV) and X-ray instruments, allowing it to catch cosmic bursts of energy across the electromagnetic spectrum, zeroing in on flares of light that other telescopes might miss.

One of its most significant detections was a gamma-ray burst — an incredibly bright blast, likely emitted by a giant star as it exploded in a supernova before collapsing into a black hole. Swift's famous image of GRB 221009A, or the BOAT ‪—‬ short for "brightest of all time" ‪—‬ looks like a speckled orange bull's-eye, caused by waves from the explosion rippling across space.

How the Swift Observatory saw the gamma-ray burst GRB 221009A, which may be the most energetic emission of this kind ever seen.

But Swift also took millions of observations of the nearby universe, including galaxies in our backyard. One of its most jaw-dropping images is this 24-hour exposure of the Andromeda galaxy (M31), located about 2.5 million light-years from Earth.

Andromeda is the closest major galaxy to ours, and it may be destined for a shared fate. Scientists suspect that Andromeda and the Milky Way are drawing closer together and might eventually collide. The merger would add Andromeda's roughly 1 trillion stars to our sky, though there probably wouldn't be any life left on Earth to appreciate it.

In Swift's view of our encroaching neighbor, captured with the observatory's ultraviolet instrument, tens of thousands of Andromeda's stars shine like sapphires set in a sparkling ring.

According to NASA, the observatory detected some 20,000 ultraviolet light sources in this image, captured over two months from May to July 2008. These sources include thousands of dense, hot star clusters scattered across Andromeda's 150,000-light-year-wide ring, as well as the distant galaxy M32 (seen as a bright orb of light to the bottom right of Andromeda's center).

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

In visible-light images of Andromeda taken with ground-based telescopes, the galaxy's bright center bleaches out many of the fiery young stars that emerge in Swift's view. While Swift likely won't be remembered best for shimmering starscapes like this one, it's a powerful reminder that looking at familiar structures in a new light can change everything.
