#6348. This armored amphibian once lived and hunted on the seafloor

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The ancient creature differs from all other known amphibians in its ability to tolerate saltwater

A Gerrothorax maritimus fossil unearthed in China was discovered in an ancient seabed, suggesting it's the first and only amphibian known to have lived in the ocean.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Most amphibians shrivel or suffocate in saltwater. But long ago, an oddball armored amphibian may have dwelled deep in the ocean.

Scientists have found evidence that an ancient amphibian with a flattened body and upturned eyes may have once stalked the seafloor. The animal, Gerrothorax maritimus, is the first ever amphibian known to have lived without access to land or freshwater, researchers report October 26 in Nature Ecology & Evolution.

G. maritimus, which lived 237 million years ago, was rather unlike today’s amphibians, which breathe and drink through their porous skin. The creature’s lifestyle was unimaginable for an amphibian, says Ryosuke Motani, a paleobiologist at the University of California, Davis. Of the more than 8,000 amphibians known today, none live solely in saltwater.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Motani and his colleagues inspected two well-preserved G. maritimus fossils from the late Triassic Period, which spanned roughly 237 million to 201 million years ago. Each creature measured around 70 centimeters, about as long as a skateboard, and was swathed in armor made of bony plates. The specimens appeared nearly identical to their closest relatives, other amphibians that dwelled in freshwater, Motani says. But the fossils’ location was unusual: They were found in what was once a seabed, roughly 30 kilometers from any ancient land.

It wasn’t clear whether the creatures lived in the ocean or were landlubbers that got buried there after they perished. So the team performed a chemical analysis. Levels of different forms of strontium in the fossil bones matched those of the Triassic ocean. This telltale sign revealed that G. maritimus ate seafood and drank seawater. “That means it lived there,” Motani says.

For amphibians, “this is the first time that that we have hard evidence that they were actually adapted for long-term life in the sea,” says Lachlan Hart, a paleobiologist at the University of New South Wales in Sydney who was not involved with the new study. Hart and his colleagues previously suggested that a different ancient amphibian may have been seafaring but probably did not dwell in the ocean.

Scientists have long searched for a marine amphibian. The fossil record is littered with skeletal fragments revealing how some mammals, reptiles and birds have adapted to a salty lifestyle. “Amphibians were always the problem because they did not really follow the rule,” Motani says.

The same skin that makes today’s amphibians vulnerable to disease and toxins also makes saltwater fearsome. Key adaptations allowed G. maritimus to skirt these issues. G. maritimus and its relatives evolved bony body armor, probably for defense. But these hard plates would have helped the seafloor dwellers prevent water loss. And unlike modern amphibians, which typically lose their internal gills after the larval stage, this creature and its close relatives retained a fishy breathing strategy suitable for life in the depths.

G. maritimus fossils hint that the animal lurked on the seafloor as an ambush predator. Its jaw lifted upward like a toilet seat so that it could unleash a suction attack on fish and other small creatures.

There may yet be other amphibians hiding in ancient oceans, environments ignored by paleontologists studying these creatures. “Because they’re amphibians, we would be looking for them in terrestrial freshwater environments,” Hart says. Perhaps there are more amphibians that have gotten their sea legs.

#6347. AI training helped some women more job interviews, but not as many as their rivals got

In a hiring test, AI training lifted interview calls for underrepresented women from 11 to 14 percent, while others got 25 percent without it.

Learning a popular skill like AI is supposed to help you get a job. But a new study found that for women who already get fewer interviews, having an AI certificate only helped a little bit.

In a London hiring experiment, it lifted their rate of interview invitations from about 11 to 14 percent.

Prospective employers invited comparable women outside those groups, with no certificate at all, to interview 25 percent of the time. The certificate narrowed the gap, but most of the gap was still there.

Nick Drydakis, an economist at Anglia Ruskin University (ARU) in Cambridge, England, ran the experiment in 2025. He directs the university’s Centre for Inclusive Societies and Economies.

Governments, employers and training providers have been promoting AI training as a route into work. Most research on AI and hiring, though, has looked at bias inside screening software.

Drydakis asked what employers do when the applicant is the one with AI skills.

Between January and June, his team answered 1,016 real job ads in London, sending three matched applications to each one. That came to more than 3,000 applications in all.

Every applicant was a fictional woman applying for a full-time private-sector job that didn’t require a degree. Each held a Level 3 vocational qualification, a practical course usually started between ages 16 and 18, plus a one-year apprenticeship.

The study ran as four separate experiments. In each, one application came from a woman in the majority group, and two came from a woman in an underrepresented group.

The underrepresented groups were Black British women, women aged 50 instead of 28, lesbian women, and women who disclosed being on the autism spectrum.

Sexual orientation showed up as a partner’s name, Helen rather than George. Autism showed up as a short line such as, “I am on the autism spectrum and known for my strong focus and attention to detail.”

One of the two applications from the underrepresented group also listed a six-month AI training certificate.

Its description covered using AI tools to automate office paperwork and handle data, aimed at the routine digital work these jobs involve.

Before any applications went out, 71 people, including HR staff, employers, students and hiring researchers, checked that each signal read clearly and that the matched applications looked equally strong otherwise.

Every application went out within a day of the ad appearing, and the team saw no sign that any employer noticed the matched sets.

Across all four experiments, prospective employers invited women from the majority groups to interview 25 percent of the time. Women from the underrepresented groups, with matching qualifications and no certificate, were invited 11 percent of the time.

The gap appeared in every experiment. Because the applications were matched, Drydakis concluded that employers were responding differently at the screening stage.

With the AI certificate, the underrepresented women’s rate rose to 14 percent. That’s about 28 percent more invitations than the same women got without it, yet still far below the majority group’s 25 percent.

“AI training can help open doors, but it should not be viewed as a substitute for fair recruitment practices,” Drydakis said.

The boost wasn’t the same everywhere. Women who disclosed autism were invited about 7 percent of the time without the certificate and 11 percent with it, against 24 percent for women who didn’t disclose.

Lesbian women’s invitation rate rose from about 13 to 18 percent, against 26 percent for heterosexual women. Both of those gains held up in the statistical tests.

For women aged 50, the rise from about 10 to 12 percent was smaller, and its statistical support depended on the test used.

The invitation rate for Black British women showed a small change, from 15 to 17 percent. Because of this small change, the experiment cannot determine whether the certificate provided any benefit at all.

The interview invitations also differed in what the jobs paid. Underrepresented women without the certificate were more often invited by employers advertising lower wages, about 7 percent lower per hour on average.

With the certificate, that pay gap shrank to about 4 percent. It didn’t disappear.

So the certificate helped in two ways, more calls and better-paid ones. However, neither brought the women level with the majority group.

Drydakis has argued in earlier work that AI skills act as a form of AI capital, something workers can build that pays off in the job market. This experiment fits that idea, up to a point.

“If we want technological change to create opportunities for everyone, investment in digital skills must be matched by strong efforts to tackle discrimination and ensure qualifications are assessed consistently across all applicant groups,” he said.

No majority-group applicant ever carried the AI certificate. That means the study can’t say whether the training would help every applicant just as much. If it did, the gap between groups wouldn’t shrink at all.

The study also stopped at the interview invitation. It didn’t follow job offers, actual pay, or how anyone was treated at work. Nor can it tell whether employers acted on prejudice or on guesses about who would do the job well.

All the applicants were women seeking jobs without a degree requirement in one city, so the results may not hold for graduate jobs, men, or other places.

A certificate that stood out in 2025 may also become routine as AI training spreads, and repeating the experiment in a few years would show whether its value holds up.

The full study was published in the journal Industrial Relations: A Journal of Economy and Society.

#6346. People blind since infancy are said to hear better, but the difference isn’t in their ears

Being blind from infancy didn't sharpen hearing in the ear itself, but it steadied how the brain judged pitch, and music lessons did the same.

People who lose their sight early in life are widely thought to hear better across the board. Yet, on a test of the ear itself, adults blind since infancy did no better than sighted adults at catching a faint tone hidden in noise.

Where they did pull ahead was in telling whether one tone was higher or lower than the next.

A computer model traced that edge to the brain, which seemed to respond to the same note more steadily from one moment to the next. Years of music lessons went with the same steadiness, in blind and sighted listeners alike.

Woon Ju Park, a researcher in the School of Psychology at the Georgia Institute of Technology, led the work with colleagues at the University of Washington. The group was small, nine blind adults and 18 sighted ones.

“Blindness is often assumed to lead to a general, across-the-board enhancement in hearing, but our findings suggest that improvements may be more specific to tasks that rely on how information is processed in the brain and not at the ears,” Park said.

The blind volunteers had lost their sight at birth or within the first two years of life. Seven could perceive no light at all, and two could sense a little light.

Each was paired with two sighted people of similar age and a similar number of years of music lessons. On average, partners were less than five years apart on both counts.

The idea that blindness sharpens hearing is old; the French writer Denis Diderot discussed it in a 1749 essay.

The pairing mattered, because many blind people have worked as piano tuners and musicians, and earlier studies that skipped it disagreed about whether blind listeners really had sharper pitch.

Everyone’s hearing was screened first at three pitches. The blind and sighted groups heard quiet tones equally well.

The first test was aimed at the cochlea, the snail-shaped part of the inner ear that sorts sound by pitch.

Listeners heard two bursts of hiss, and one of them hid a steady tone vibrating 1,200 times a second. They pressed a key to say which burst held the tone.

The hiss had a gap cut around the tone’s pitch, and the gap changed width from trial to trial. How quickly people improved as the gap widened shows how finely their ears separate nearby pitches.

Blind and sighted listeners scored almost exactly alike, after 80 practice trials and two sessions of 480 trials each. The gap between the groups was far smaller than the smallest difference the test was built to catch.

The tie on the ear test ruled out two other explanations. The team hadn’t simply recruited blind people with unusually good ears.

And the blind volunteers probably weren’t just paying closer attention, since both groups made careless misses at about the same low rate.

In the second test, listeners heard two short tones, one after the other, and said whether the pitch went up or down, 216 times each.

On a piano, neighboring keys sit one-twelfth of an octave apart. The pitch gap between the two tones ranged from one and a half keys down to about a tenth of a key.

The tones lasted anywhere from a third of a second to about two hundredths of a second.

Here, the blind listeners had the edge, and their lead grew when the pitches sat farther apart and the tones lasted longer.

So their edge was clearest when each sound gave them plenty to work with. The authors suggest that may help explain why earlier studies disagreed: one that used shorter tones found no advantage.

Next, the team built a computer model of how a brain might hear each tone, with two settings.

One was tuning, how narrowly the brain’s pitch-sensing cells respond around a single note. The other was jitter: play the identical tone twice and the brain’s response still wobbles a little. Researchers call that wobble internal noise.

Fitted to each person’s answers, tuning came out the same in both groups, and internal noise was lower in the blind listeners.

A 2019 brain-scanning study had found slightly narrower pitch tuning in blind people’s hearing regions, but only by about 3 percent. The authors judged that change too small to be the main cause.

When the researchers forced both groups to share one level of internal noise, the model’s fit got much worse. Forcing them to share one tuning width cost far less.

Most of the blind listeners’ advantage came down to steadier responses, not narrower tuning, and that result surprised the team.

In an interview with Earth.com, Park explained that hearing can become more precise in more than one way. The auditory system can respond more distinctly to different sounds, or it can respond more reliably to the same sound each time.

“We often think of better perception as being able to distinguish sounds more sharply from each other,” Park said. “But our findings suggest that responding more consistently may be just as important.”

Because the volunteers had a wide range of music experience, the team could also check what lessons did. People with more years of musical training had lower internal noise, whether they were blind or sighted.

Blindness still predicted lower internal noise after the researchers accounted for music experience. Music didn’t explain the blind listeners’ advantage away.

Neither blindness nor training predicted a better score on the ear test. That cuts against earlier reports of sharper tuning in musicians’ ears, and the team had enough people to catch an effect that size.

Blind listeners were still generally better at telling pitches apart than sighted musicians, Park said. What surprised the team was that both groups seemed to improve in the same way.

“There’s been a long-standing question about whether superior hearing in early blind individuals comes from the absence of vision or from their extensive auditory experience,” Park told Earth.com.

“Our findings suggest that both may play a role. Auditory experience appears to improve pitch perception in a way similar to musical training, while early blindness may provide an additional benefit.”

Asked whether everyday listeners could lower their own internal noise with training, Park said it is possible. Studies of vision have shown that learning to tell objects apart can reduce internal noise.

The noise can come from many different sources, Park added, and how or why it falls with training is still not fully understood.

“These findings suggest that learning may involve making our sensory representations more consistent and reliable,” Park said.

The study can’t tell whether the blind listeners’ steadier hearing comes from the loss of vision itself or from years of leaning harder on sound.

The internal noise in the model also isn’t a direct recording of brain cells. It stands for how much a person’s judgment wavers from one try to the next.

One explanation the authors offer is that practice teaches the brain which signals to trust and which to ignore. Their model can’t yet separate that from other possibilities, such as more precise timing in how the brain encodes sound.

Park said the study relied on relatively simple listening tasks and a mathematical model. The next step is to find out what is happening in the listeners’ brains.

“Do their patterns of brain activity reflect what we found in behavior? Are there changes in brain structure that help explain their improved hearing?” Park said.

To pull vision loss apart from heavy listening, the authors suggest checking whether blind people’s advantage is larger for hearing sounds that matter most in their everyday lives.

The full study was published in the Journal of Neuroscience.

#6345. An ancient camp in Alaska holds amazing clues about how the first people traveled all the way to North America

Ice Age people who crossed the Bering Land Bridge built a lean-to, an earth oven, and a sewing kit at an Alaska camp 13,800 years ago.

The Bering Land Bridge is usually described as a temporary highway that Ice Age hunters walked across to get to the Americas.

On a bluff above the Tanana River in interior Alaska, though, some of those people stopped and stayed a while. They put up a shelter, dug a cooking oven, and sewed with bone needles. Furthermore, they came back to the same spot for up to two centuries.

The camp is 13,800 years old, and its shelter is the earliest potential case of a built dwelling anywhere in North America.

The people who used it weren’t a small hunting party passing through. They were a group of related families, and they knew the land well enough to fetch stone from 230 miles away.

Kelly Graf, a professor in the Department of Anthropology at the University of Kansas, leads the dig. The site is called Shég’ Xdaltth’í’, which means “they were there” in Alaska Native Athabascan.

In an interview with Earth.com, Graf said the finds suggest the site was “a place where the folks here lived and considered it their home.”

The camp is about 34 miles (55 kilometers) south-southeast of Fairbanks, on a bluff roughly 115 feet (35 meters) above the Tanana River. A bedrock knob behind it blocks the northwest wind.

Since 2016, Graf’s team has worked a single excavation block of 269 square feet (25 square meters). This is the same area as the floor of a one-car garage.

Radiocarbon dates put its finds in three Ice Age layers. The oldest, from about 13,800 years ago, is the one this study is about. That layer alone has produced more than 80,000 pieces of stone, bone, and charcoal.

In that oldest layer, the team found a large oval of charcoal-stained ground at least 10 feet (3 meters) across, packed with thousands of small artifacts and bones.

The team read it as most likely a lean-to that opened to the south. It had a hearth near its center and a shallow pit full of refuse beside it.

A stone slab about 8 inches (20 centimeters) on a side lay inside the shelter, and Graf counts it among her favorite finds.

“It was sitting within a dwelling feature, and all around it were really bashed-up bison bones. And there were a lot of quartz and quartzite-rock hammerstones – which were the hammers they used to break the bones,” Graf said.

“So we think they were using these stones to fully process the bones to extract marrow and likely to render grease. This was all happening near a large earth oven,” she added.

The oven was a bed of charcoal more than 4 feet (1.2 meters) across, holding 230 fire-cracked rocks. It had a cap of earth covering it, possibly making it suitable for slow cooking.

The oldest layer produced nearly 7,000 bones, most broken into fragments. Researchers at the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology, in Germany, used protein signatures to identify the bone fragments.

They found 373 pieces that came mostly from steppe bison, with mammoth, horse, caribou, hares, foxes, a lynx also present. Some were bones from different types of birds, including grouse and swans.

Graf told Earth.com the camp would have held a group of related, extended family members making up a few households. They refurbished stone tools and broke down carcasses around open-air fires.

The bone tools say the same thing. The team found eight fragments of sewing needles, four still carrying part of the eye, along with an awl tip and an antler pendant with a drilled hole.

Waterfowl bones hint at summer visits, and fox and lynx bones at winter trapping. The camp may have been used in more than one season.

The camp has no storage pits and none of the dug-in houses seen at permanent Ice Age sites in Siberia, though. So Graf’s team calls the people here semi-settled rather than settled near the Bering Land Bridge.

The stone came from a wide area. All 25 pieces of obsidian trace to one source, Batza Téna, about 230 miles (370 kilometers) to the northwest.

One piece of rhyolite, tested at Texas A&M University, came from Triple Lakes in what is now Denali National Park.

Six finished tools stand out. They’re flaked on both faces into a diamond shape, and most have a stem with edges that were ground smooth. These could have been bound to form a handle or shaft.

The team hasn’t yet examined them for wear, so it won’t yet call them spear points or knives. For now they are hafted bifaces.

“It’s the only site in Alaska that features this clear diamond shape,” Graf said.

“And the only other places at this time that have such points in a northern context are on the Russian side of the land bridge. It suggests people traveled across the Bering Land Bridge to and possibly from this location.”

The Russian sites she means, Nikita Lake and Berelekh, also lack the tiny stone blades called microblades that mark Swan Point, the oldest site in the same river basin.

Graf’s team proposes that the two toolkits belonged to two separate migrations out of northeast Asia across the Bering Land Bridge.

At least 15 of the bones belonged to wolves. One lower jaw was measured against dire wolves from the La Brea tar pits, Ice Age wolves from Alaska, and modern gray wolves, and its shape fit none of them.

The team thinks it belonged to a population unlike any wolf known from Alaska, ancient or modern.

Asked by Earth.com what surprised her most, Graf named the sheer amount and variety of tools, food, and features. A habitation site like this one is rare in the late Ice Age, she said.

She also named “the wolf remains that suggest familiarity with humans and resources they can gain from a relationship with humans.”

Genetic studies suggest Siberian wolves gave rise to the first dogs in North America, so the people of Shég’ Xdaltth’í’ may have kept dogs.

Wolves and the earliest dogs leave bones that are hard to tell apart, though, so that stays a suggestion for now.

Several of the features extend into the walls of the excavation block, so the lean-to and the oven have each been only partly uncovered.

The bigger question is who these people were. Geneticists expect that several distinct populations lived in Beringia, the region around the land bridge, at the end of the Ice Age.

Settling which of them lived here will take ancient genomes, Graf’s team said. Until those are recovered, the link between the toolkit and a particular people stays a hypothesis.

“The next step is completely excavating the features we have only partially uncovered. We need to test our hypotheses about site use,” Graf said. “It would be excellent to find another dwelling feature!”

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances.

Archaeologists found a small cemetery full of high-status burials, two of which may be the graves of Germanic chieftains.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists excavating in northeastern France have unearthed a small fifth-century cemetery containing the graves of two Germanic chieftains and two warhorses. The burial ground is providing new information about the transitional period after the fall of the Roman Empire.

The burial complex was discovered near the city of Colmar, just a few miles from the Rhine River, which forms the border between France and Germany. This area had a Gallo-Roman village from the first to the third centuries, and archaeologists found several ancient houses, hearths, wells and craft areas, according to a Nov. 6 translated statement from the French National Institute for Preventive Archaeological Research (Inrap).

Archaeologists also uncovered a rare fifth-century cemetery at the site, which was used from about A.D. 450 to 500, a critical time period in Western Europe because of the collapse of the Roman Empire. While scholars have debated for centuries about why the empire fell, one key issue was the repeated occupation of Rome in the fifth century by Germanic tribes known as the Goths and the Vandals.

Several of the burials included gold-and-garnet accessories on weapons and clothing.

Archaeologists discovered 11 adult graves, three graves of children and two horse burials at the site, according to the statement. In two of the female burials, archaeologists found silver bird-shaped brooches, glass bead necklaces and a bone comb, suggesting that these may have been high-status women.

But two of the male burials, in particular, stood out because of their high-quality grave goods, including a sword with a partially preserved wooden scabbard, a shield, a javelin and a scramasax, a type of Germanic short sword, which was decorated with a gold-and-garnet accessory. The weapons are characteristic of the burials of Germanic chieftains or mercenaries, according to the archaeologists, and two horses were buried nearby with their harnesses.

Two horse burials were discovered in the cemetery.

In addition to the weapons and warhorses, archaeologists noticed evidence on the men's bones that hinted that the individuals were likely warriors. Two people suffered stab wounds that showed no signs of healing, which suggests they died quickly and violently, according to the statement. And another man's right knee bones had completely fused together, which would have prevented him from bending it. This condition, called ankylosis, commonly results from an improperly healed injury.

The archaeologists believe the warrior's grave goods weren't just for show, but further study of the skeletons is planned to confirm whether the injuries seen during the excavation could have been sustained in a conflict.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Few Germanic settlements and cemeteries from the fifth century have been found, so the newly excavated site should provide important information about the upheavals linked to the fall of the Western Roman Empire and how that political collapse affected communities on the edge of the empire.

#6342. Scientists finally link human fossils found in China fifty years ago to the Denisovans, early human ancestors that we still know very little about

Two bones from Xujiayao, dug up in China in 1976-79 and dated to 199,000-138,000 years ago, yielded 18 proteins that point to Denisovans.

Between 1976 and 1979, excavators in the Nihewan Basin of northern China recovered 20 human fossils at a site called Xujiayao. From there, it took nearly five decades to tie them to the Denisovan lineage, an extinct human group first identified from DNA in a Siberian cave.

The finds included pieces of skull and jaw and some teeth, buried with animal bones and artifacts that were mostly scrapers and spheroids. Researchers later filed them under five different names.

A team that includes Song Xing and Qiaomei Fu of the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology (IVPP) in Beijing has now recovered 18 ancient proteins from two of those bones.

One small change in a collagen protein points both to the Denisovan lineage, although the proteins cannot show which Denisovan population the people belonged to.

Uranium-series and electron-spin-resonance dating place the Xujiayao layer at around 199,000 to 138,000 years ago. The first studies noted a thick skull vault and teeth that resembled those of Neanderthals.

Those early descriptions led scientists to call the people Homo sapiens neanderthalensis, early Homo sapiens or archaic Homo sapiens. When the arguments over sapiens stalled, some papers fell back on the neutral term archaic Homo.

A later study of the partial skull called Xujiayao 6 measured a braincase of about 1.8 quarts (1,700 milliliters). That unusually large figure made the skull the type specimen of a proposed species, Homo juluensis, one of several new names listed in a 2024 article in Nature Communications.

The name placed Xujiayao in a group apart from the Homo longi skull from Harbin and from fossils at Dali and Jinniushan. The new paper argues against that divide.

Animal bones from the same layer came first, and they gave a positive result for ancient protein. Next came the human fossils, a right parietal bone from Xujiayao 6 and a piece of the Xujiayao 14 mandible, labeled PA1490 and PA1497 in the lab. Each went through a 3D scan before anyone touched it with a drill.

Researchers in protective gear drilled one small hole in each bone in a clean room at the institute’s Molecular Paleontology Laboratory. They wrapped the surrounding surface in aluminum foil and kept the holes as small as they could.

The powder went into hydrochloric acid and then a 149-degree Fahrenheit (65-degree Celsius) bath for three hours, which split each sample into three fractions.

Empty blanks ran alongside to catch contamination, and the bone of a modern Bactrian camel went through the same steps.

Two labs read the fragments on mass spectrometers, one at Capital Medical University and one at Fudan University in Shanghai.

One software search returned 15,194 unique peptides, the short chains of amino acids that make up proteins, across the two samples.

Old proteins carry a chemical wear called deamidation, and the team used it to separate ancient material from modern traces. Keratins and the trypsin used in the lab showed far less of it.

After further filtering and a check in a second software program, 18 proteins remained, 13 in the skull bone and 15 in the jaw.

The decisive signal sits in COL1A2, one of the chains of type I collagen, the main protein in bone. At position 996, Neanderthals and modern humans carry the amino acid arginine.

Every Denisovan tested so far carries lysine there instead, according to the paper. That reference group consists of two individuals from Xiahe, Penghu 1, the Harbin skull and Denisova 3 from Siberia.

Both Xujiayao bones showed lysine. The skull bone gave 57 peptides with the variant and the jaw gave 61, while each sample gave only one low-quality peptide with arginine.

The researchers then built a family tree from 2,074 amino acid positions in eight proteins, adding Neanderthals, 50 present-day people and a chimpanzee for comparison. Xujiayao grouped with Denisova 3 and other Denisovan-related individuals with a probability above 99 percent.

Xujiayao ranks “among the earliest molecularly confirmed Denisovans,” the authors wrote in Nature. Similar protein work identified a jaw from a Tibetan Plateau cave at Baishiya Karst in Gansu, dated to at least 160,000 years ago.

With the fossils assigned, the team compared their anatomy against other human relatives, using CT scans at a resolution of 37.56 microns.

They took 26 linear measurements, three angles and two indices from the Xujiayao 6 skull. C.-H. Chang shared a 3D model of the Penghu mandible, and X. Wu allowed the scanning of casts from Xuchang and Hualongdong.

Parts of the skull look like Homo erectus. The vault measures 0.30 inches (7.7 millimeters) thick at the top of the head and 0.47 inches (12 millimeters) at the parietal bulge, and the braincase is low and wide.

Other parts look more recent. A strongly arched temporal bone also appears in later species, including modern humans, while the inner-ear layout and, in the Xuchang fossils, a small pit at the back of the skull recall late Neanderthals.

The mix also has its own signature. The authors list a low skull with nearly parallel side walls, a massive brow ridge, a flat cheek region and a lower face that barely juts forward.

The paper reaches beyond Xujiayao. Its authors compared the anatomy with the Harbin skull known as Dragon Man and a jawbone from Penghu, off Taiwan, and they assigned most of East Asia’s late Middle Pleistocene fossils to the Denisovan lineage, including Jinniushan, Dali and Hualongdong.

The team also rejected the brain-size argument for Homo juluensis. Braincases in that group hold 1.8 to 1.9 quarts (1,700 to 1,800 milliliters) and the other East Asian fossils 1.2 to 1.5 quarts (1,120 to 1,420 milliliters), but modern humans alone span 1.15 to 2 quarts (1,090 to 1,880 milliliters).

If shape and molecules count together, the authors argued, Denisovans lived in East Asia from at least 300,000 to 45,000 years ago. The authors linked their disappearance from the region to a major migration of modern humans around 40,000 years ago.

The authors wrote that adding other skulls gives “a nearly complete picture of the cranial morphology of Denisovans.” That portrait is a composite.

Its account of a sloping forehead, square eye sockets and a broad nasal opening relies on facial bones from Harbin, Jinniushan, Hualongdong and Dali, and it also matches features predicted from Denisovan DNA.

Only Harbin among those four has molecular confirmation in the paper. Jinniushan, Dali and Hualongdong join the lineage on shape alone, and the authors note that the full set of traits does not appear together in any single specimen.

The protein evidence also has limits. It rests on one reliable variant, known from five reference individuals, and it comes from two of the 20 Xujiayao fossils. Within the Denisovan branch, individuals formed an unstable arrangement with probabilities below 50 percent.

A test for a variant specific to Penghu produced no reliable result, so the team placed Xujiayao only in a late Middle Pleistocene East Asian Denisovan population. The 1970s excavators left the bones with a site name, and a drill hole in each of two pieces has now added a lineage.

The full study was published in the journal Nature.

#6340. An Egyptian villager working near his house discovered the buried remains of two colossal pharaoh statues

A villager's discovery in Egypt led archaeologists to two colossal royal statues, including a confirmed Ramesses II figure once about 28 feet tall.

A resident of Behbeit El-Hagar, a village in Egypt’s Gharbia Governorate, was working a plot he owns in front of his house. There he found a strange inscription on a stone block, and he reported it right away.

From there, a rescue excavation by Egypt’s Supreme Council of Antiquities (SCA) uncovered the remains of two colossal royal statues. Egypt’s Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities announced the finds on October 13, 2026.

One statue is confirmed as Ramesses II. Its head alone stands about 5.2 feet (1.6 meters) high.

Behbeit El-Hagar lies in the central Nile Delta. The village holds the ruins of a major temple to the goddess Isis, according to the Metropolitan Museum of Art.

The resident alerted the local antiquities inspectorate. Inspectors examined the stone and confirmed that it was an ancient artifact, and the SCA sent a specialist team to excavate the spot.

Tourism and Antiquities Minister Sherif Fathy praised the resident for reporting the stone immediately. He said public involvement is key to protecting Egypt’s heritage for future generations.

Fathy called the discovery an important addition to Egypt’s recent finds. In his view, it sheds further light on the history and archaeological significance of Behbeit El-Hagar.

The block that started the search is pink granite, about 4.3 feet (1.3 meters) long. Its hieroglyphs preserve two royal titles of Ramesses II.

One is Nesu-bity, or “King of Upper and Lower Egypt.” The other is Sa-Ra, or “Son of Ra.”

Dr. Hisham El-Leithy, secretary-general of the SCA, described the first statue. The king wears the Double Crown, which symbolized the unification of Upper and Lower Egypt.

The upper part of the statue’s back pillar also survives. It is inscribed with the king’s Horus name, Hor-ka-nakht-mery-maat, often rendered as “Strong bull, beloved of Maat.”

Based on the size of the head, El-Leithy estimated that the complete statue stood about 28 feet (8.5 meters) tall, including its base. The estimate rests on proportions, since only parts of that statue have been recovered.

Ramesses II, whose monuments include a Luxor obelisk now in Paris, reigned for 66 years. His rule, from about 1279 to 1213 B.C., fell within the 19th Dynasty of Egypt’s New Kingdom.

The second find is the main body of a royal statue, about 7.9 feet (2.4 meters) long. Its legs and base are missing.

This figure wears the nemes, the striped royal headcloth, and part of its top is lost. The face remains clear and well preserved.

Those features resemble the first statue’s, and archaeologists believe the second figure may also depict Ramesses II. That identification has not been confirmed.

The granite block lay roughly 3.3 feet (1 meter) north of this second statue.

Excavation and study will continue at the site, El-Leithy said. The goal is a clearer picture of the statues, the area’s history and its architectural development.

The Isis temple at Behbeit El-Hagar is much younger than Ramesses II. Nectanebo II, who ruled from 360 to 343 B.C., built most of it in dark granite, in a severe style typical of his dynasty’s Delta temples.

That work came roughly 850 years after Ramesses II’s reign ended. Nectanebo II decorated only one important chapel before the second Persian invasion of Egypt.

The temple probably replaced an earlier one begun in the 26th Dynasty. Ptolemy II later completed the sanctuary and chapels, and Ptolemy III added a hypostyle hall and the western facade.

The temple collapsed sometime after Ptolemy III and before the early third century A.D. Weak foundations may have played a part, and an earthquake, possibly in 24 B.C., may have brought it down.

Blocks from the temple have reached museums abroad. One granodiorite relief at the Met shows Nectanebo II offering incense and a collar to the god Osiris.

The ministry’s announcement does not connect the two statues to the Isis temple.

Ramesses II had statues of himself made across his empire. Among them are seated figures about 69 feet (21 meters) tall at Abu Simbel.

His mortuary temple, the Ramesseum, stood on the West Bank at Thebes, modern Luxor. One colossal seated figure there was carved from a single block of granite quarried near Aswan, according to the British Museum.

The surviving head and torso, now in London, measure just over 8.2 feet (2.5 meters). The complete seated figure would have reached roughly 23 feet (7 meters).

A red granite sphinx found at Memphis carries Ramesses II’s titles, but his sculptors reworked it from an earlier king’s monument. Flinders Petrie excavated it near the temple of Ptah in 1913.

The sphinx’s original owner was erased so thoroughly that he is unlikely ever to be identified. Ramesses II’s son and successor, Merenptah, later added his own cartouches to its shoulders.

The information was obtained from Egypt’s Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities.

Neuroscientists say people can be "trained" to recognize when they're dreaming — in other words, lucid dreaming may be an acquirable skill.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

During dreams, bizarre scenes you encounter can seem as tangible as reality; you feel as though you're really flying through the sky or being chased through a jungle of bright-purple trees. But in special cases, people realize they're in the midst of a dream as it's unfolding.

Called lucid dreaming, this phenomenon occurs when we suddenly regain our capacity for metacognition, or thinking about our own thoughts, in the middle of a dream. Lucid dreamers can sometimes even control the content or trajectory of their dreams. Now, researchers claim that they've found a way to "train" people to lucid dream by having them meditate and complete virtual-reality-augmented exercises while they're awake.

In a study involving a few dozen participants, the scientists found that repeating this training twice a week for a month significantly increased how often participants experienced lucid dreaming. They say the approach could have practical applications as an intervention for people with nightmares, anxiety or post-traumatic stress disorder — but those applications are theoretical, for now.

If you could learn how to lucid dream, would you? Let us know in the poll below, and add your thoughts in the comments.

#6338. Voyager 1 went silent in deep space right before reaching a historic milestone of one ‘light day’ away from Earth

NASA briefly lost contact with Voyager 1 in October 2026. The signal returned just weeks before the spacecraft reaches a historic milestone.

On Oct. 18, 2026, the antennas of NASA’s Deep Space Network tried to pick up Voyager 1 during a scheduled contact and found nothing. A second attempt 24 hours later also failed.

The signal came back on Oct. 20, and the team at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) in Southern California has kept in touch with the probe since then.

NASA schedules Nov. 18 as the day Voyager 1, already the farthest human-made object, reaches one light-day from Earth, according to JPL. They had not previously said what caused the October problems.

The Deep Space Network has large antennas at Goldstone in California, near Madrid in Spain and near Canberra in Australia. The largest dish at each site measures about 230 feet (70 meters) across.

Those antennas handled the two contact attempts in October. Mission controllers logged no detectable signal on Oct. 18 or Oct. 19.

Kareem Badaruddin, the Voyager mission manager at JPL, said the episode was new to his team. “This is the first time we’ve seen the spacecraft do something like this,” he said in the JPL statement.

He also said the mission has reached a stage where the team has “to expect the unexpected.” The probe has surprised its operators before, including the time it began talking through a radio system not used since 1981.

After contact returned, the team worked out that one group of thrusters on the spacecraft had gone offline and that a backup group had turned on.

The onboard computers carry instructions to make that swap by themselves when they detect a problem with the active thrusters.

JPL calls this kind of automatic reaction fault protection. It puts the probe in a safe, stable state and pauses normal operations so that engineers on the ground can study the problem.

In March 2025, engineers revived a set of roll thrusters that had stopped working in 2004.

Early in September, about six weeks before the probe dropped out of contact, JPL engineers sent the commands that turned off three devices on Voyager 1 and turned on three lower-power substitutes.

Inside the team, the job goes by the name Big Bang. The devices double as a source of warmth for the spacecraft, so JPL could not do them one at a time and all three changed at once.

Voyager 2 got the treatment first, and NASA reported on Aug. 4, 2026 that the swap there should keep three instruments powered for at least one more year. An instrument on Voyager 2 would otherwise have gone dark before the end of 2026.

Nothing in the Oct. 29 note ties the September commands to the thrusters.

Both probes run on radioisotope generators, which turn the heat from decaying plutonium into electricity. The output on each probe falls by about 4 watts a year and, with margins now thin, JPL has been shutting off whatever is not essential.

Ten science instruments went up on Voyager 1 in 1977. A NASA status page updated in April lists only two still running on it, the magnetometer and the plasma wave subsystem.

Controllers switched off the cosmic ray subsystem on Feb. 25, 2025, in one of a series of shutdowns meant to stretch the remaining power. The low-energy charged particle instrument was next, on April 17, 2026.

Without the Big Bang swap, another Voyager 1 instrument would likely have been turned off as early as summer 2027, JPL said.

Voyager 1 launched on Sept. 5, 1977, two weeks after its twin, passed Jupiter and Saturn, and entered interstellar space in August 2012. It is moving at about 38,000 miles per hour (61,155 kilometers per hour).

NASA’s light-day page sets the crossing on Nov. 18, when the probe will sit about 16.09 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers) from Earth.

Light covers the distance to the Moon in 1.3 seconds. Artemis II astronauts needed about three days for the same trip.

NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory explains how far away Voyager 1 is when it reaches one light-day from Earth. Credit: NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory.

Voyager 2 took a different route so it could visit Uranus and Neptune, and NASA expects it to reach the same distance in November 2035. The nearest star system, Proxima Centauri, lies about 4.24 light-years away.

Voyager project manager Suzanne Dodd described what the distance does to a conversation. “If you want to say ‘hello’ to Voyager, you send your message and then you go home and you wait two days before you finally get a response,” she said in the JPL statement.

JPL’s Oct. 29 note does not say what knocked the thrusters offline, and engineers are still investigating. It also does not confirm that the thruster switch was what interrupted the signal.

The note does not name the three devices replaced in September or give the amount of power saved. It also says nothing about when the mission might end, although the team expects more surprises before summer 2027.

The light-day crossing itself will change nothing on board or around the spacecraft, JPL said. Its value lies in showing the length of the mission and the size of the distances involved.

At one light-day, a command sent from Goldstone, Madrid or Canberra needs a full day to reach Voyager 1. The answer needs another.

The information was obtained from NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory.

#6336. This may be the best evidence yet that dinosaur blood can fossilize

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Minerals may have preserved remnants of ancient blood in a dinosaur bone, but some are skeptical

Using a technique called scanning electron microscopy to peer inside an 115 million-year-old dinosaur limb bone, researchers captured images of tiny ellipsoid structures, about 20 micrometers in diameter, that may be fossilized red blood cells. Molecular analyses found preserved heme — the oxygen-carrying component of hemoglobin — in the bone.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

The life and times of a dinosaur may be written in its blood — if blood can be preserved in bone.

Tiny microstructures found in the limb bones of a fossilized 115-million-year-old specimen are the remnants of red blood cells, researchers report November 2 in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. The team says these are both the oldest red blood cell structures yet identified and the first to be chemically proven. But not everyone is as sanguine about that conclusion.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The ability to identify such structures could offer a powerful molecular window into the physiology of long-extinct animals, including their metabolism and even activity levels, says paleontologist Kliti Grice of Curtin University in Bentley, Australia.

The bone, from a fossil-rich site in northeastern Brazil called Mina Pedra Branca, belonged to the dinosaur Aratasaurus museunacionali. Grice and her colleagues used a variety of chemical and imaging analyses to study the Cretaceous Period specimen.

Maurilio Oliveira/Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 4.0)

The team prepared thin cross-sectional slices of bone and imaged details of the limb bone’s internal structure with focused electron beams. That revealed ellipse-shaped microstructures within the limb’s fossilized network of blood vessels.

A map of the ellipsoids’ chemical element composition revealed that they were full of iron, carbon and nitrogen, all components of a biomolecule called heme. Heme is an iron-bearing, ring-shaped molecule found in hemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen throughout the body.

Then, the researchers used a technique that identifies molecules by how they scatter laser light. Those analyses suggested the presence of porphyrins, ringlike organic compounds found in blood — and the precursors of heme. Finally, they ruled out contamination from other porphyrins, such as the pigment chlorophyll, by separating and identifying the molecular contents of a bone extract. That experiment also suggested heme.

Taken together, these findings point unequivocally to the preservation of molecular traces of ancient blood, the team says. They also offer a clue to a novel pathway that might preserve those traces for so many millions of years.

Blood cells decompose within days of the death of an organism. Only unusual and fast-acting environmental and biochemical conditions could have stopped decay and held those tissues in place as the organism fossilizes.

In this fossil, the secret ingredient was a manganese oxide mineral called hausmannite, the researchers say. The team’s analyses had found the mineral within the ellipsoid structures. That mineral, they propose, may have acted as a time capsule, preserving the cellular structures and protecting the molecules within, including collagen amino acids.

Distinguishing fossilized blood cells from nonorganic minerals that formed within a fossil after the organism’s death is a tricky task. During fossilization, mineral-rich fluids seep in and around the bones, and the minerals that form within the fossil can bear a strong resemblance to bodily structures.

In a 1997 study, two paleontologists analyzed tiny spheres found inside the limb of a fossil, possibly a pterosaur. The spheres were once thought to be the fossilized remnants of ancient blood cells, but the duo determined that the spheres were instead pyrite, an iron mineral that had been deposited in the bones after death.

Those paleontologists suggested that, going forward, several criteria should be met before proposing a blood cell origin for fossilized structures, including comparing the shape of the structures with that of living related organisms and identifying certain biomarkers in the structures. One of those biomarkers is heme compounds.

Grice and her colleagues say that their study meets these criteria. Unlike the pyrite, hausmannite was crucial to preservation, “rather than simply a mineral that replaced biological material after it had disappeared,” she says. The close spatial relationship between the hausmannite, the blood cell-like structures and the chemical signatures of heme “raises the possibility that mineralization helped stabilize, entomb and protect components of the original biological material during fossilization.”

But Mary Schweitzer, a paleontologist at North Carolina State University in Raleigh who was not involved in the new study, says she doesn’t think these findings do fully meet those criteria.

The heme biomarkers, for example, don’t appear to be localized to the round structures alone, as would be expected in fossilized blood cells, but come from analysis of the entire bone. The proposed red blood cells also differ in size and shape compared with red blood cells from living birds and reptiles, she says.

Schweitzer is no stranger to skepticism over the discovery of ephemeral tissues in fossils. In 2005, she and her colleagues reported the first recovery of flexible, soft-tissue blood vessels from the 68-million-year-old fossilized leg bone of a Tyrannosaurus rex. It was a landmark study that sparked debate, including over how it would even be possible to preserve such tissues through deep time, as well as the most surefire way to detect them in the present.

“I am not convinced” that the research team has definitively identified heme compounds, Schweitzer says. “I do applaud them for bringing a plethora of methods to the study. Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence, and that does require state-of-the-art technology.”

No one really knows what a dinosaur’s red blood cell shape would be, let alone how the process of fossilization might distort the original shape of the structures, or allow heme-related molecules to escape their cellular confines over time, Grice says.

And, she says, her team’s interpretation of the evidence doesn’t just rely on the observations of those structures. “[It] rests on the convergence of anatomy, morphology, mineralogy, elemental analysis and molecular chemistry,” she says. “That combination is critical.”

As for whether other fossils might have molecular traces that have been preserved by hausmannite, “we simply don’t know yet,” Grice says. “But this type of preservation may not be quite as rare as we currently think.”

Questions or comments on this article? E-mail us at feedback@sciencenews.org | Reprints FAQ

K. Grice et al. Heme signatures in mineralized red blood cells within vascular canals of a 115-million-year-old dinosaur bone. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. 2026. doi: 10.1073/pnas.2614248123

D.M. Martill and D.M. Unwin. Small spheres in fossil bones: Blood corpuscles or diagenetic products? Palaeontology. 1997.

#6335. Scientists got a much better look at endangered red pandas by putting cameras in trees

The red panda has a false thumb, and there's a good reason for that. To photograph a shy wild animal, researchers usually set up a motion-sensing camera near…

To photograph a shy wild animal, researchers usually set up a motion-sensing camera near the ground and wait for the animal to walk by. For red pandas, a camera placed near the ground misses a lot, because these endangered animals live mostly up in the trees.

At 19 sites in eastern Nepal, cameras about 16 feet (5 meters) up in trees took eight times as many pictures of red pandas as cameras near the ground. With cameras in the trees, researchers can watch an animal that is very hard to spot in the wild.

Sonam Tashi Lama of the Red Panda Network, a conservation group, led the work with Kathryn Bugler, James Ross, and Adrian Paterson at Lincoln University in New Zealand.

“Red pandas are very elusive,” Lama said. In eastern Nepal, oak trees are often covered in a reddish moss, and a red panda’s reddish fur blends into it. Researchers sometimes mistake pieces of moss for red pandas from a distance.

Lama said the camouflage helps protect red pandas from predators. Those predators likely include clouded leopards and common leopards, and sometimes yellow-throated martens, tree-climbing animals that usually hunt in pairs.

The same camouflage makes red pandas hard to study. Their behavior in the wild hasn’t been studied much, because the animals are so difficult to find and follow.

Researchers in earlier studies watched red pandas in person, fitted them with GPS tracking collars, or looked for their droppings. Lama’s team tested whether cameras could help, and whether they work better near the ground or in the trees.

From late 2017 to mid-2018, the team set up 19 pairs of motion-sensing cameras, known as camera traps, in the forests of eastern Nepal. Each pair stayed in place for at least a month.

The team picked trees that red pandas were already using. Fresh droppings and feeding marks showed which trees those were. Local people called Forest Guardians, who monitor red pandas for the Red Panda Network, helped choose the sites.

One camera in each pair was mounted on a tree trunk, about 16 inches (40 centimeters) above the ground. The other was placed up in the branches, about 16 feet above the ground.

There’s a reason for that height. Red pandas leave their droppings at regular spots in trees, and those spots are about 16 feet up on average.

Together, the cameras took almost 60,000 pictures. More than three-quarters of them showed no animal at all. Moving leaves and the heat of sunlight can set off a camera’s sensor, and that happened far more often in the trees.

Red pandas appeared in only 903 pictures, at 11 of the 19 sites. The tree cameras took 807 of those pictures, and the ground cameras took 96.

The team also counted how many separate times a red panda showed up. Tree cameras recorded 38 appearances. Ground cameras recorded 21. But a single appearance in a tree could produce a long series of pictures.

In one case, the team wrote, a tree camera recorded a single red panda over a period of 2 hours and 18 minutes. In that time, the animal slept in different positions, groomed itself, and explored its surroundings and the camera.

Red pandas sometimes investigated the tree cameras, but they didn’t touch them. One camera, aimed down a tree trunk, recorded a red panda climbing down headfirst.

The pictures also showed red pandas active at all hours of the day and night. The animals were busiest between 4 and 6 in the morning. They eat constantly, Lama said, taking only short naps between meals of bamboo.

Putting a camera in a tree is harder than setting one up near the ground. Reaching a tree camera takes a ladder or climbing gear. The team wrote that each one also took about 30 minutes longer to set up and to check.

The Forest Guardians are skilled tree climbers, Lama said. Tree cameras also took many more pictures with no animal in them, which gave the team more pictures to sort through.

Even so, the team wrote that the extra effort is worth it, because wild red pandas have been so difficult to observe. They recommended that researchers who want to monitor red pandas mount cameras in trees, about 16 feet up.

At that height, a camera can show whether red pandas are present, when they are active, how they behave, and possibly which predators are nearby. At one site in this study, a marten was photographed in a tree that a red panda often visited.

Ground cameras still have a use, the team wrote. They can record red pandas, but they are better suited to recording the other mammals that live on the forest floor.

Pictures from the tree cameras were clear enough to show the markings on each red panda’s face. Those markings differ from one animal to the next, so researchers can use them to tell red pandas apart.

Local populations of red pandas in Nepal are very small, typically 20 to 50 animals. Lama’s team didn’t use the pictures to estimate how many red pandas live in the study area. In future studies, the team wrote, the face markings could make that kind of estimate possible.

Biologists often estimate how many animals live in an area by learning to recognize individual animals, then recording how often they see the same ones again. The method is called mark-recapture.

The next question is whether that method works for red pandas. To make the animals easier to identify, the team suggested aiming cameras so they capture a red panda’s whole body.

The full study was published in the journal Wildlife Society Bulletin.

This tiny inkwell contains an alphabetic inscription in ancient Etruscan, a language that has never been fully decoded.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The chicken-shaped, black-glazed vase has an abecedarium ‪—‬ an inscription with the 26 letters of the Etruscan alphabet in order.

What it is: A bird-shaped ceramic inkwell

This small terra-cotta vase, which is shaped like a cockerel or young male chicken with human feet, was discovered in central Italy and was made by the ancient Etruscans. The potter inscribed the Etruscan alphabet on the body of the chicken, giving modern researchers clues to a language that has never been fully deciphered.

The vase stands just over 4 inches (10 centimeters) tall and is in the collection of the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York City. The dark-black ceramic, known as bucchero, was made through a unique firing method that prevented the kiln from getting enough oxygen, which caused the clay to absorb carbon. Bucchero is considered the trademark Etruscan ceramic, and it was produced from the seventh to the fourth centuries B.C. by this pre-Roman society. It is unclear where the cockerel vase was originally found, but it may have been discovered in a grave in one of the many cemeteries that surround Viterbo, which was originally an Etruscan town about 50 miles (80 kilometers) northwest of modern-day Rome.

According to The Met, the vase may have been a portable inkwell used by an ancient Etruscan who was learning how to write. The cockerel's head was the stopper, and it was loosely attached to the body by a cord through a set of loops. The inscription on the body of the vase is known as an abecedarium ‪—‬ the sequential list of letters in an alphabet.

The Etruscan alphabet is well known, since it was adopted from a regional version of the Greek alphabet in the early eighth century B.C. There were 26 letters in the Etruscan alphabet, but one of them in this abecedarium is incorrect. A close look at the end of the alphabet shows that someone inscribed an S twice; the second one should look more like an X, according to The Met.

The terracotta cockerel vase was one of several ancient Etruscan artifacts that helped experts partially decode the mysterious ancient language, as it preserved the order of the letters in the early alphabet, archaeologist Gisela Richter wrote in a 1930 catalog of The Met's classical artifacts.

Thanks to the adoption of the Greek alphabet, it's possible to fully sound out the Etruscan language. But although more than 10,000 Etruscan inscriptions have been found, the language is still only partially understood because those inscriptions are short and any lengthy Etruscan literature that once existed has been lost.

#6332. Deadly eel virus can spread in a surprising way

Scientists found that infected European eels can spread a dangerous virus through bites, raising new concerns for conservation.

A herpesvirus that kills European eels can jump from one fish to the next when they bite each other.

A Belgian study provides the first evidence that biting can transmit this virus.

Fish live in water, so the assumption has been that their viruses travel through it too. For plenty of aquatic diseases, that holds up. But anguillid herpesvirus 1 does not last well outside its host.

At 77°F (25°C) about 90% of its infectivity had gone within 12 hours in lab tests. The mucus coating an eel’s skin works against it as well.

The virus spreads between eels all the same. A team led by Natacha Delrez at the University of Liège says biting may help explain how.

When infected and healthy eels were made to bite one another, every healthy animal involved became infected. That held whether the contact was at the mouth or the tail, and whichever animal did the biting.

The fish were anesthetized and kept in laboratory tanks. So the work shows a bite can pass on the infection.

Whether that happens regularly in the wild is left open.

Infected tissue in fish is normally located by examining organs after the animal has been euthanized.

The method gives detailed information. But it does not allow one infection to be followed in the same living animal.

Delrez and her colleagues inserted two genes into the virus.

One of them was a firefly gene for light production. In eels infected with the altered virus, tissues where it was multiplying emitted a faint glow.

The light is invisible to a person looking at the animal, but specialized imaging equipment picks it up.

The images recorded which parts of the body were infected first and where infection appeared later.

The modified virus was compared with the original. Growth rates in cell cultures were the same.

Disease symptoms and mortality in infected eels were comparable. On that basis the team used the altered virus for the rest of the work.

Four strains were used at first, collected in the Netherlands, Denmark, and the United Kingdom. Genome analysis was done with the MRC-University of Glasgow Centre for Virus Research.

One strain was used in the later experiments, which reduced the number of animals needed.

Age turned out to matter. European eels arrive on the continent’s coasts as glass eels, tiny and close to transparent. They darken once they push into rivers and other inland habitats.

Then they settle into a yellow eel stage, which may go on for years of feeding and growing before the final migration back to sea.

Glass eels held in contaminated water showed no detectable infection.

Among slightly older juveniles, infection was detected in one of six animals on both day three and day six, and in two of six on day nine.

Yellow eels did worst, with all six animals infected within six days.

Imaging put the earliest signals in the gills and in tissues inside the mouth, areas around the teeth and lips among them.

That detail became important later. In three separate waterborne exposure experiments, all yellow eels showed symptoms between days eight and 12. About 20% died.

The virus appeared to enter at the mouth and gills. But in eels kept together, imaging showed glowing patches elsewhere.

The patches were farther down the body, particularly around the tail. They did not match the pattern seen earlier.

Yellow eels housed in groups of 20 were then compared with infected yellow eels housed individually.

At nine days, group-housed eels had several glowing patches around their heads and tails. Eels housed alone had visible signals around the mouth and gills and none along the rest of the body.

Solitary eels were still seriously infected. Tests found virus in internal organs, including the brain and heart. They lacked only the separate patches on the outer body.

The team turned to behavior. Yellow eels generally live alone, can defend territory aggressively, and sometimes bite one another when sharing limited space.

Eel farmers documented the behavior decades earlier. They described bites around the mouth and nips at the tail, particularly in crowded conditions.

The patches were in those same locations. Some, the researchers proposed, had developed where another infected eel had bitten.

They were not part of the ordinary progression of the disease. The team tested that directly.

For the biting experiments the eels were anesthetized. Three kinds of contact were then arranged between infected and healthy animals.

In one, an infected eel bit a healthy eel around the mouth. The other two involved the tail. The healthy eel delivered the bite in one case, the infected eel in the other.

The healthy animals were afterward placed in separate tanks, which ruled out further biting between them.

Every one became infected, and some showed glowing tissue three days after the bite. The team took that as strong evidence that the physical contact itself could transfer the virus.

Handling might still have moved contaminated mucus or water from one fish to another by accident.

To separate that from the bite, they washed the heads or tails of infected eels in small quantities of water. Healthy animals were then exposed to the wash water.

Much less infection followed. None of the healthy eels tested positive three days after exposure to the head-washing water, and two showed weak signals at six days.

In the biting experiments, every exposed animal was infected. A bite, the team concluded, does more for the virus. It is not simply moving a little contaminated water from one animal to the next.

None of this rules water out. The team drew water from a tank of 15 infected eels and transferred it to tanks of healthy fish.

All six exposed animals became infected. So did all six when the water had been standing for 24 hours.

The picture changed once the scientists started diluting.

Water diluted a hundredfold infected five of six eels while fresh. Twelve hours later the same dilution reached only three animals, and a day later it reached none at all.

Water diluted ten-thousandfold and left to stand for 12 hours caused no detectable infection in the tested eels.

Infectivity also dropped fast in ordinary water, and eel skin mucus cut it further.

Viral concentration helps determine whether water spreads the disease.

A crowded eel farm keeps it high. A river does the opposite: the water moves, the virus thins out, and fish may be far apart. A bite skips all of that.

Numbers matter too. Young eels reaching European coastlines are now at roughly 1% of early-1980s levels, a fall linked to dams, overfishing, pollution, and climate change.

In a tank, under anesthesia, with the bites arranged by hand, anguillid herpesvirus 1 passed from eel to eel every time.

What eels get up to in a river is harder to know. Their interactions are difficult to observe. Little is known about how often they bite one another at today’s reduced population densities.

What the researchers will say is that nothing like it has been reported before.

They call this the first case of a virus spreading between members of the same fish species through biting in water.

No one has yet documented a naturally occurring bite that transmitted this virus between two wild eels.

The findings raise concerns for eel farms, where animals are housed together and aggressive encounters may be more likely.

Restocking programs worry the authors for a related reason. Young eels are sometimes raised or held together, then released into rivers that may already contain infected animals.

European eels are critically endangered, and dams and other barriers divide their remaining river habitats.

Protecting them means understanding diseases, not just releasing more fish.

Researchers suggest exploring vaccines for farmed eels and conservation programs that move young glass eels into rivers.

The findings show that the virus may spread through more than water. A bite between eels can also pass it on.

The full study was published in the Journal of Virology.

#6331. Alzheimer’s discovery reveals a breakdown in the brain’s defenses

A mouse study reveals how the Alzheimer’s-linked gene CASS4 helps brain immune cells surround plaques and limit nearby nerve damage.

An immune cell can’t do much for damaged brain tissue if it can’t get there. That problem seems to lie at the heart of a new study on CASS4, a gene linked to Alzheimer’s disease.

Mice without CASS4 had less contact between their brain immune cells and the protein clumps associated with Alzheimer’s.

Bigger clumps, looser packing and more damage followed, although the brain still had about as many immune cells to work with.

Microglia, as these cells are called, crawl about in brain tissue checking for damage and collecting waste. Those clumps are called plaques.

For over a decade, genetics studies have pointed to CASS4 without explaining much about its work in a living brain.

It belongs among the Alzheimer’s risk genes that do their work outside nerve cells, despite nerve cells bearing the damage most of us know about.

Adeline Walsh, a physiology graduate student at the University of Virginia, led the research with neuroscientist John Lukens. He heads a lab at the university’s Center for Brain Immunology and Glia.

“Despite CASS4 being an Alzheimer’s risk gene, really nothing is known about what this gene does or how it affects the brain during disease. Our lab sought to address this major knowledge gap with this paper,” Walsh said.

The work points to CASS4 as a possible drug target. Alzheimer’s affects more than six million Americans and ranks sixth among the country’s causes of death.

For the plaque experiments, the team needed mice that would grow amyloid deposits while still young.

They used mice carrying five mutations associated with inherited Alzheimer’s disease, then removed CASS4 from some of them.

A separate characterization of the strain found plaques arriving sooner and more consistently in females, hence the choice to use females throughout.

In mice without CASS4, the cortex and the memory-related hippocampus both had extra buildup by five months old.

The largest size group, over 1,000 cubic micrometers, accounted for more deposits in those brains.

More swollen nerve endings surrounded each plaque, and a second marker of nerve fiber damage was elevated in both brain areas.

At four months old, 10 mice from each group had a swimming test. Somewhere in the cloudy water was a platform to stand on, hidden just under the surface.

For four days, both groups found it at about the same pace, and both did equally well on a memory test the next day.

Then the platform moved to the far side of the pool, and the mice missing the gene began to struggle.

The mice went back to where the platform used to be, and swam farther from the new location than the other mice did.

The team took the platform out for a final test, and these mice still spent more time at the old position than the new one.

They covered as much water, just as fast, as the other mice, and two tests of activity and anxiety came out much the same.

Mice without Alzheimer’s mutations showed no such difficulty after losing CASS4, suggesting that the effect depended on the disease model.

An old habit can be hard to shake for people with Alzheimer’s, and researchers have much left to learn about it.

Of course, a swim in a pool doesn’t capture what it’s like for a person.

Differences in microglial numbers did not explain the findings. Mice without CASS4 had about as many microglia as their littermates with the gene intact.

A check of cell division, and of the signs of cells going on alert near a plaque, found much the same in each group.

The cells also swallowed labeled amyloid at much the same rate.

Within 10 to 20 micrometers of a plaque, though, the mice without CASS4 had much less microglial material. That distance is a fraction of the width of a human hair.

Reduced microglial contact was accompanied by less rounded, less densely packed plaques, with amyloid spread loosely around the core.

A 2015 study described that packing job. Microglia put a barrier around a plaque and squeeze the protein into a tighter clump, so less of it can reach the neighboring nerve cells.

There was still something to sort out. Every cell in the first mice had lost CASS4, which left open where the trouble really started.

In another group, two weeks of medicated food after weaning switched CASS4 off in cells bearing a particular surface marker.

After a few weeks, blood cells with working CASS4 had replaced the affected blood cells, but microglia live for years and stayed without the gene.

The second group again had more plaques in the hippocampus, more of the largest deposits and more damage to nerve fibers nearby.

Those plaques were less round and less densely packed, despite the brains having no shortage of microglial material compared with the controls.

“Many in the field initially presumed that CASS4 was likely functioning in neurons to influence Alzheimer’s. Our findings shift this paradigm by proving that CASS4 predominantly acts through the immune system,” Lukens said.

Pulling a cell across a surface is a job for tiny gripping points, and the protein made from CASS4 helps organize them.

The protein acts as a scaffold for structures called focal adhesions, which help cells grip their surroundings.

The team found 98 genes working at different levels in microglia without CASS4, with less activity in systems that build and tighten the fibers used to move.

A separate test with 1,318 antibodies picked out 93 differences in phosphate tags, little chemical additions that control proteins, with 17% involving proteins central to focal adhesion signaling.

Grown in a dish, these microglia spread less of a key gripping protein beneath them. A scratched layer of related immune cells also took longer to close the gap.

Through a window in the skull, the team watched how microglia responded to a tiny brain injury created with a laser.

Normal microglia sent branches toward it over the next 40 minutes, and the ones missing CASS4 hardly stirred.

People aren’t mice with CASS4 deleted. We inherit small differences in its DNA, and the team still needs to find out what those differences mean for the protein.

Mice with human versions of the gene would help, including versions that turn its activity up. They’d still be mice, of course, with all the limits of studying human disease in another animal.

“We are now actively exploring potential roles for CASS4 in multiple other neurodegenerative disorders and developing novel strategies to therapeutically target it,” Lukens said.

There’s no drug to boost CASS4 yet, or evidence that doing so slows Alzheimer’s in people.

Getting a treatment into microglia and following what happens to plaques over time would be necessary steps along that road.

The study is published in the Journal of Experimental Medicine.
