#6330. Lowe’s vs. Home Depot Black Friday Deals

After scouring both websites, we like deals that are a little simpler and help you spend less instead of maximizing your total “savings.”

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Stop stacking up tools and appliances in your wishlist and get ready to pull the trigger. Black Friday sales are live for tons of top items, including power tools, hand tools, larger appliances, and more at Lowe’s and Home Depot. That said, between the two established hardware stores, which one is offering better deals?

The answer is complicated and boils down to a few key questions: What exactly are you looking for, and how much do you need? While both offer discounted power tools, Home Depot offers its biggest savings when you buy multiple items. Lowe's, on the other hand, focuses more on traditional discounts on single tools. Take a look at some of the sales we highlight below.

Before you read on, it’s important to clarify that both retailers offer bundle deals, straight discounts, and buy-one-get-one offers. In fact, they even have a few sales that are quite similar to one another like the DeWalt cordless 20-volt drill which is 80 dollars off the retail price at both Lowe’s and Home Depot.

However, a lot of the best deals we saw at Lowe’s were simple discounts while Home Depot had a lot more based on getting additional tools free with purchase.

We typically lean toward Lowe’s over Home Depot because that simplicity tends to leave more money in your wallet. If all you’re buying is one drill, you can get it on sale at Lowe’s without needing to buy a single additional item to maximize the savings. While you might not save the same percentage compared to the retail price, you’ll spend fewer total dollars, which, to us, feels like the true bottom line.

For instance, this Craftsman nailer that is $60 off comes with no charger or battery. If you already own Craftsman power tools, this is no problem at all. In fact, it lowers the total price of your purchase.

Similarly, the Craftsman steel tool chest, which is being discounted $120 doesn’t come with additional hand tools or accessories. Just a plain old tool chest at a massive discount.

If you want to reset your tool selection, Home Depot offers deals on larger bundles. Many of its best Black Friday sales aren’t standalone discounts; they’re built around add-ons. If you buy one combo kit, you can get an additional power tool from the brand for free.

A great example of this is the Milwaukee combo kit. It includes a Packout rolling toolbox, a hammer drill, an impact driver, a grinder, and a reciprocating saw, plus two batteries and a charger. On top of the 42 percent discount, the kit includes a “free” 18-volt battery pack that typically retails for around 230 bucks. This further adds to the savings, but it comes with the caveat of making a large, multi-tool purchase.

Shopping at either Lowe’s or Home Depot during Black Friday will get you a ton of good deals. You can’t make a serious mistake either way. However, we lean a little more toward Lowe’s because it's often cheaper overall if you only want a few specific items. The best savings will come from buying only what you need instead of chasing the biggest discounts. Lowe’s offers the best chance to leave without feeling like you got a few fluff pieces you didn’t really need.

#6329. Seabirds that nest together spend winter thousands of miles apart – and DNA may predict where

Seabirds that share nesting sites can winter thousands of miles apart, with their genes helping guide their migration.

Two seabirds can nest side by side and leave for winter at about the same time. You might expect them to fly together. In the western Mediterranean, they often do not.

Cory’s shearwaters and Scopoli’s shearwaters nest in the same colonies in parts of the western Mediterranean and leave on migration at about the same time each fall.

A new study found that birds from those shared colonies generally wintered in areas typical of their own species.

Some ended up thousands of miles from their neighbors, while hybrids tended to travel intermediate distances.

The results suggest that genes shape these birds’ routes more than their colony neighbors do.

Beñat Garcia-Urdangarin, a doctoral student at the University of Barcelona, is the study’s first author.

Raül Ramos and Jacob González-Solís, who heads the university’s Seabird Ecology Lab, are among the lead authors.

The team tracked the migrations of 50 breeding shearwaters and sequenced the genomes, or complete sets of DNA, of those birds and eight others.

Only seven of the 58 birds were hybrids. For that reason, the team wrote, the hybrid result should be interpreted cautiously.

Across most of their ranges, the two species breed apart. Cory’s shearwaters nest mainly on Atlantic islands such as the Azores, Madeira and the Canaries.

Scopoli’s shearwaters nest on small islands across the Mediterranean, as far east as the Aegean Sea.

The two species separated about 350,000 years ago. Today their ranges overlap around the Alboran Sea, the part of the western Mediterranean closest to the Strait of Gibraltar.

Garcia-Urdangarin’s team worked in that overlap zone, at four colonies where both species nest. For comparison, the researchers also sampled a Cory’s colony in the Canary Islands and a Scopoli’s colony on Zembra Island in Tunisia.

Why would neighbors matter? Some migrating birds do learn routes from each other. Pink-footed geese set up a new migration route and breeding area within a decade. Birds from the original population switched to the new route.

Shearwaters that copy their neighbors should winter where the rest of their colony winters, whatever their ancestry. With an inherited route, each bird should follow its ancestry instead.

Each bird wore a small light sensor on one leg for a year or two. The sensor recorded light levels. The team used the timing of each dawn and dusk to estimate the bird’s position twice a day.

The estimates are rough. Each one can be off by a couple hundred miles (a few hundred kilometers).

When the researchers recovered a sensor, they took a blood sample from the bird. The blood was used to sequence its genome. That genome showed how much of the bird’s ancestry came from each species.

From 2008 to 2020, the team recorded 127 migrations, including eight by the same shearwater.

The tracks are available through the Seabird Tracking Database.

The two single-species colonies showed what each species normally does.

About 70% of the trips tracked from the Canary Islands ended off southern Africa, along the Agulhas Current and the area where it meets the Benguela Current.

Most trips tracked from Tunisia ended in the tropics instead, around the Gulf of Guinea and the equatorial Atlantic.

In the mixed colonies, most birds went where their own species goes. Palomas Island, a colony of fewer than 100 pairs, had only one tagged Cory’s shearwater.

That bird flew to the Agulhas Current four years in a row, while every Scopoli’s shearwater tracked from the same island wintered along the tropical African coast.

The team’s statistical model estimated that Cory’s shearwaters from the mixed colonies traveled about 7,200 miles (11,660 km) to their wintering areas.

For Scopoli’s shearwaters there, the estimate was about 2,100 miles (3,340 km). Both figures are for males. Females of both species traveled almost 1,900 miles (3,000 km) farther.

A few Cory’s shearwaters from the mixed colonies did winter off West Africa, in food-rich waters heavily used by the other species. But Cory’s shearwaters from colonies outside the overlap zone are known to winter there too.

The team also found seven recent hybrids in the mixed colonies, 17.5% of the birds sampled there. Two were first-generation hybrids, with one parent from each species. The rest had mostly Scopoli’s ancestry.

Six of the seven hybrids were tracked. Four of them wintered off Namibia and the other two off West Africa.

For hybrid males, the model’s estimate was about 3,800 miles (6,060 km). That distance falls between the estimates for the two species.

“This provides solid evidence that the long-distance migrations of these species have a genetic basis,” Ramos said.

In-between routes have been reported before, in songbirds. A past study found hybrid songbirds taking routes between those of their parent populations.

Birds tracked across multiple years tended to travel similar distances each year.

In the team’s model, differences among individual birds accounted for 82% of the variation in travel distance.

The authors suggested that this habit builds up over time. A young bird starts with an inherited tendency, then refines the route as it gains experience.

Young shearwaters have years to gain that experience. They typically begin breeding at about nine years old.

Earlier tracking studies found that young Cory’s shearwaters shortened and straightened their routes as they aged.

The two species may also meet in their wintering areas. Both seabirds use the food-rich waters off West Africa, Angola and Namibia.

Birds that mix there may later settle in a colony of the other species, the team proposed.

González-Solís said conservation strategies need to consider the zones where the two species breed together, including the transfer of genes between species there.

For now, the hybrid result rests on nine migrations by six birds.

That is too few to test how the trait is inherited, or to compare first-generation hybrids with birds whose ancestry is mostly Scopoli’s.

Hybrid wintering areas also looked more like those of Scopoli’s shearwaters than those of Cory’s shearwaters, the authors wrote.

Every tracked bird was also a breeding adult, so the study didn’t follow young birds on their first migrations.

The next question is which parts of the genome are involved.

The team wrote that finding them will take many more tracked and sequenced birds, sampled across the full breeding ranges of both species.

The full study was published in the journal Molecular Ecology.

#6328. Mysterious gas on Mars suggests magma below

Something is leaking from the ground near one of Mars’ largest volcanoes, and scientists think it’s a sign that active magma is buried below.

In a study published Nov. 4 in Science Advances, researchers report detections of hydrogen chloride (HCl) gas within 6 miles (10 kilometers) of the planet’s surface near the volcano Alba Mons. Notably, the detections came during aphelion, when Mars is farthest from the Sun and HCl is typically absent from its atmosphere. The location and out-of-season timing combined with the site’s unique geology likely point to volcanic outgassing — gas escaping from magma as it rises toward the surface — the authors argue.

“It seems that we are showing that there may still be more heat inside Mars than we thought, enough heat to have still fluid magma at depth,” co-author Daniel Mège, a professor at the Space Research Centre of the Polish Academy of Sciences, tells Astronomy.

The detection adds to mounting evidence, including recent detections of marsquakes, that the martian interior is not the dead world scientists once assumed. While scientists know volcanism influenced the planet’s evolution, it has remained unclear whether it continues today.

There’s no question that igneous activity shaped Mars into the planet we see today. Between 3.7 billion and 3 billion years ago, eruptions flooded the planet’s surface with vast lava plains. Later volcanic activity built some of the solar system’s largest volcanoes, including the roughly 16-mile-high (25 km) Olympus Mons — the tallest — and the 4.2-mile-high (6.8 km) Alba Mons, the largest by surface area. Though it rises just 4.2 miles (6.8 km), Alba Mons sprawls roughly 870 by 620 miles (1,400 by 1,000 km).

Those colossal peaks formed not through shifting plate tectonics like on Earth, but through stagnant-lid tectonics. Mars’ outer shell is a single rigid plate, meaning magma repeatedly erupted at the same sites, piling lava to towering heights over millions of years.

Many of these giants, including Olympus and Alba Mons, sit atop Tharsis, a volcanic plateau roughly 3,000 miles (5,000 km) across. Some lava flows at Tharsis are relatively young, dating back only tens of millions of years, yet there has been no definitive evidence for ongoing volcanic activity at the plateau or on the planet as a whole. Nevertheless, the case has been slowly building.

Before its mission ended in 2022, NASA’s InSight lander recorded more than 1,300 marsquakes. Quakes alone don’t prove volcanic activity. “Marsquakes can happen for multiple reasons, only one of which is faulting or other tectonic activity around volcanoes,” says R. Aileen Yingst, a senior scientist at the Planetary Science Institute who studies Mars geology and was not involved in the study. For example, some of the marsquakes InSight detected were caused by meteoroid impacts. And a cooling and contracting crust can cause seismic activity without magma.

Most of the quakes, though, were traced to a system of young volcanic fissures — long, parallel cracks where the martian crust was once pulled apart by rising magma — called Cerberus Fossae. Deposits of volcanic ash at Cerberus Fossae date to as recently as 53,000 years ago. Some scientists argue the large number of marsquakes in this setting could hint that magma is still moving below. In 2022, researchers proposed that a 2,500-mile-wide (4,000 km) active mantle plume lies beneath the Elysium Planitia region that surrounds Cerberus Fossae. On Earth, such columns of hot solid rock rise from deep in the planet’s interior, melting rock and creating magma, which could explain both the marsquakes and the ash deposits.

Orbiters searching for evidence of active volcanism on the martian surface have yet to turn up anything conclusive, the authors say. Sulfur dioxide (SO₂), the gas most often used to track volcanoes on Earth, has never been detected on Mars at concentrations that would point to magma. But that absence doesn’t mean Mars’ magma has gone quiet. Measurements at volcanoes on Earth show that SO₂ dominates during eruptions but drops sharply between them, when HCl becomes the more abundant gas. “[A]s long as we do not observe an active lava flow, or lava fountain, or explosion on Mars, we do not expect SO₂ emissions to be very high,” Mège says. Mars is also about 2.5 times richer in chlorine than Earth, and some martian volcanic meteorites are “up to four times richer” in chlorine than sulfur. “All this suggests that HCl is the best gas to look for on Mars if we want to identify active magma at depth that is not being erupted,” Mège explains.

The detections in the study come from the Atmospheric Chemistry Suite (ACS), a set of three infrared spectrometers aboard the Trace Gas Orbiter, a joint mission of the European Space Agency and Russia’s space agency, Roscosmos. The orbiter began science operations in 2018. ACS’s spectrometers analyze the sunlight filtering through the martian atmosphere, picking out the wavelengths each gas absorbs to reveal what’s in the air and at what altitude. In 2020, ACS made the first detection of HCl on Mars. It appeared planetwide during the warm, dusty season near perihelion, reaching concentrations of 4 to 5 parts per billion. Researchers attributed the presence of that HCl to chemical reactions involving dust, ice, and water vapor in the atmosphere during the warm season, not to volcanic activity.

What’s different about the new finding is that they detected HCl not at perihelion, but near aphelion, when the gas is otherwise absent from Mars’ atmosphere. The HCl was also localized above an interesting geological location: the region around the sprawling, low-profile volcano Alba Mons, located on the northern edge of Tharsis. After two tentative detections in one Mars year, a dedicated search two Mars years later turned up six more, mostly northeast of the volcano. The gas hugged the lowest 6 miles (10 km) of the atmosphere at concentrations up to 1.5 parts per billion.

The team ruled out atmospheric processes for the HCl and considered three possible ground sources: volcanic activity, mud volcanism, and the breakdown of chlorine-bearing salts called perchlorates. Mud volcanoes — likely inactive for billions of years — are widespread across Mars’ northern lowlands, so they alone couldn’t explain why the gas showed up in only one isolated place. And even if mud volcanism were active and releasing the HCl, it would likely still point to magma beneath the surface. Perchlorates are likewise found across the northern lowlands, which rules them out on the same grounds. “[I]f this mechanism were involved, HCl would be detected throughout the northern hemisphere, it would not be local,” Mège says. That leaves localized volcanic activity, which fits with models of the planet’s formation suggesting HCl should be among the most abundant gases in its volcanic emissions.

To gather more data, the team turned to high-resolution images from the High Resolution Imaging Science Experiment (HiRISE) camera aboard NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, and the Colour and Stereo Surface Imaging System (CaSSIS) aboard the Trace Gas Orbiter. They were looking for features near Alba Mons that could explain the seepage. They found a grouping of several narrow fissures that had not previously been identified. Many were just tens of centimeters wide, and some extended for up to 6.21 miles (10 km) long. Some were ringed by dark halos, suggesting material may have recently been ejected from within. The fissures were so thin that seasonal dust and ice activity should have already covered them up unless something was actively keeping them open. The authors did not confirm that the HCl came from the fissures, but they suggest the cracks may run from the icy ground near the surface all the way down to magma. Gas rising through them could escape directly or become trapped in the frozen ground, seeping into the atmosphere over time as the ice turns to vapor.

The case isn’t closed. The team didn’t catch gas escaping from any specific fissure. And although the cracks hadn’t been described before, they appear in older orbital images, with no visible changes between then and now. The authors stop short of a firm conclusion, saying only that ongoing volcanic activity is the best explanation for what they found. “What we can say today is: when we consider all the alternatives, it is the best explanation,” Mège notes. The next step is to keep watching. Future searches could reveal more hidden pockets of gas, and with them, more signs that Mars’ interior is still stirring. Ultimately, “to confirm the source,” Mège says, “we would need someone or some robot to check, with a very multidisciplinary payload.”

If there is still magma beneath Alba Mons, the implications reach beyond geology. Mars is smaller than Earth, so it should have shed its internal heat faster. “If it’s the case that Mars is still volcanically active, then the thermal models of Mars would probably need to be revisited,” Yingst explains. And where magma meets groundwater, hydrothermal systems – the kind of environment where life on Earth may have first emerged – usually follow. If conditions stayed stable long enough, Mège says, life could have arisen there. And “if these stable conditions continue until now, then these living organisms may still be there, somewhere below the surface.”

Brooks Mendenhall is a staff writer at Astronomy, based in Chattanooga, Tennessee, fueled by an unending curiosity about the universe. A former classroom teacher, he has a knack for breaking down complex concepts for a wide audience.

#6327. A high-fiber diet may clear away plastic in the gut

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Mice that ate lots of fiber had far less particles accumulate in the body

A diet that includes high-fiber foods, like these vegetables, might come with a surprise benefit. Fiber could help carry nanoplastics out of the body, suggests a new study in mice.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Here’s a new reason to eat your beans and greens.

A high-fiber diet may help sweep plastic particles from the gut, researchers report October 15 in Nature Communications. In mice that ingested plastic, eating loads of fiber daily kept the particles from piling up in the intestines. The finding hints at fiber’s power to protect the body from environmental garbage, says Eddy Y. Zeng, an environmental scientist at South China University of Technology in Guangzhou.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Researchers have long known that fiber can improve our health, in part by lowering cholesterol, keeping blood sugar levels in check and easing food through the gut. But now, Zeng says, his team’s results suggest an additional benefit.

We live in a world littered with plastic, much of it too small to see. These micro and nanoplastics, shed by disposable water bottles, fast food containers and other worldly junk, can make their way into our bodies. It’s not completely clear what such shards do to our health, but we have some hints. Scientists have linked plastic particles in people’s arteries to increased risk of heart attack and stroke. And mice that ingest tiny bits of plastic can show signs of organ injury.

Zeng’s team thought dietary fiber might provide some defense. Fiber forms a complex network of polymers that could trap ingested plastics like flies in a spider web, he says.

The researchers put mice on low-, medium-, or high-fiber diets, then fed them plastic particles. Over the next 24 hours, the medium- and high-fiber groups of mice cleared more particles from their bodies than their low-fiber counterparts, the team discovered. That’s important, Zeng says, because these particles can do damage. After a week of daily plastic feedings, his team saw gut tissue damage — but only in the low-fiber group. Experiments in test tubes suggest that fiber physically wraps around and sticks to plastic particles.

It’s too soon to say if dietary fiber does the same in humans. Zeng’s study was performed in mice and not tethered to realistic fiber numbers. Though mice in the high-fiber group ate far more fiber than what what’s recommended for people, he thinks the findings are worth pursuing in follow-up studies.

And even if fiber doesn’t end up purging plastic from people’s guts, Zeng says, it probably wouldn’t hurt for us to add a little more to our diets.

Questions or comments on this article? E-mail us at feedback@sciencenews.org | Reprints FAQ

Z. Yu et al. High fiber diet mitigates exposure risk of nanoplastics in male mice. Nature Communications. 2026. doi: 10.1038/s41467-026-78675-7

In a key coastal area of Peru, violence was low despite the practice of human sacrifice.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Despite engaging in human sacrifice, the people who lived in the Lambayeque Valley of northern Peru had low levels of violence, a new study of their remains finds.

Human sacrifice occurred in the valley over the millennia. It's thought that at least some of these mass sacrifices were attempts to appease the gods in the wake of El Niño, a periodic weather phenomenon that can lead to intense rains and flooding in Peru and droughts in other parts of South and Central America.

"We have one example at the site of Sicán where around [A.D.] 1050/1100, around 200 individuals were killed and ritualistically buried during an intense El Niño event," study co-author Haagen Klaus, an anthropology professor at George Mason University in Virginia, told Live Science in an email.

Other human sacrifice findings include more than 200 children found near the modern-day town of Huanchaco who were sacrificed sometime between 600 and 800 years ago, possibly during an El Niño.

However, despite the occurrence of human sacrifice, levels of violence unrelated to sacrifice were actually quite low in the Lambayeque Valley. In the study, scientists analyzed the skeletal remains of 1,519 people from the Lambayeque Valley who lived between roughly 1500 B.C. and A.D. 1800, and whose remains were preserved enough to detect signs of violent trauma, including interpersonal violence.

A skull showing blunt force trauma that dates to the Chimu period, roughly 1375 to 1490.

Of these skeletons, "only 25 (1.6%) exhibited traumatic lesions consistent with interpersonal conflict, and 77 exhibited post-cranial traumatic lesions consistent with accidental trauma (5.1%)," Klaus and co-author Thomas Snyder, a bioarchaeologist at New York University, wrote in the paper, which was published Nov. 8 in the journal Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology.

The team didn't find any link between a person's sex and violence, they noted. The findings mean that despite the presence of human sacrifice, the amount of violence unrelated to sacrifice was low. This leaves a question: Why?

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

A healed fracture on the left leg of a person who lived sometime between 1000 to 650 B.C. The fracture may have been from an accident.

"Ritual violence may have alleviated non-ritual violence by creating spaces where social tensions could get worked out in a few different ways," Klaus said.

It's important to remember that other areas of Peru also practiced human sacrifice but didn't have the same low levels of interpersonal violence. Klaus noted that areas in the Peruvian highlands sometimes had higher rates of interpersonal violence. In their paper, Klaus and Snyder noted that societies that originated in the highlands, such as the Tiwanaku, Wari and Inca had to grapple with poorer soils and cold temperatures, and these challenges may have been a factor in increasing the levels of interpersonal violence.

The "evidence of sub-lethal and lethal violence forceful enough to break bone is significantly higher in some areas of Peru's highlands," Klaus said. He and Snyder noted in their paper that the inhabitants of the Lambayeque Valley may have had better access to marine and water resources, such as seafood and rivers that could be used for agricultural irrigation, than those who lived in highland areas. Access to these resources may have helped alleviate interpersonal violence in the valley by providing more food resources, they wrote.

Aside from practicing human sacrifice, people in the valley may have engaged in other practices that helped lower levels of interpersonal violence, researchers who were not involved in the new study told Live Science.

Environmental conditions may have helped reduce conflict or there could be "really unusual cultural practices in this region of avoiding or mediating conflict — both between and within groups," Elizabeth Arkush, an anthropology professor at the University of Pittsburgh, said in an email.

Constanza Ceruti, an anthropologist and explorer with the National Geographic Society, said in an email that she's glad that researchers are studying human sacrifices "after decades of being ignored as a taboo topic in academic discussion." She praised the study’s large sample size and noted that human sacrifice is a "phenomenon primarily associated [with] the manipulation and concentration of power by elites."

Jordi Rivera Prince, an anthropology professor at Tulane University, said that the findings dovetail with her excavations in the region, where she has "found little evidence of violent trauma during the Salinar (400-200 BCE), a period of great social change in the Andes."

Weston McCool, an archaeology professor at Cal Poly, said in an email that the newly published paper "is an interesting study that provides additional evidence for a sharp break in patterns of violence between the Andean coast and highlands." He noted that it "supports the hypothesis that coastal populations were buffered from terrestrial environmental downturns in ways that highland populations were not. The nature of that resilience, however, remains an important question for future research."

Snyder, T. J., & Klaus, H. D. (2026). Pax Lambayeque? Trauma, interpersonal violence, and environment over 3,000 years in the Lambayeque Valley Complex, Peru. Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology, 5, 1889466. https://doi.org/10.3389/fearc.2026.1889466

Owen Jarus is a regular contributor to Live Science who writes about archaeology and humans' past. He has also written for The Independent (UK), The Canadian Press (CP) and The Associated Press (AP), among others. Owen has a bachelor of arts degree from the University of Toronto and a journalism degree from Ryerson University.
